subtopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
I would like to make a statement to the house regarding questions. It is not generally known that oral questions
are not permitted under any rule in this house. Standing order 44 provides for placing questions on the order paper seeking information relating to public affairs, and it adds that if any member requires an oral answer he may distinguish his question by an asterisk. In former years a few urgent questions were orally addressed to the government on the orders of the day being called, but now all kind of questions are asked at that stage of the proceedings. Most of them could be placed on the order paper. Even newspaper clippings and telegrams, the accuracy of which has not previously been ascertained, are then read and included in the official report of debates. This practice is resorted to on the ground that it is followed in the United Kingdom House of Commons. There could be no greater mistake. The rule at Westminster is quite different from that, and it could be followed with advantage by this house. Our standing order No. 1 provides that:
In all cases not provided for hereafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
What is the custom today in the United Kingdom house? I cannot find it in a better place than in the 14th edition of May's "Parliamentary Practice", published a year ago under the control of Sir Gilbert Campion, K.C.B., present clerk of the United Kingdom house. Let us quote what he says at page 332:
Notice of a question to a minister or other member is usually placed upon the notice paper, unless the question relates to a matter of urgency or to the course of public business. The custom formerly in vogue, of giving notice of questions by reading the question aloud, is no longer allowed, unless the consent of the Speaker in the case of any particular question has been previously obtained. Notice of a question is given by delivering the terms thereof in writing to the clerks at the table during the sitting of the house.
This is the same as our standing order 44 respecting written questions. But with regard to oral questions, the same authority says at page 340:
Questions which have not appeared on the paper, but which are of an urgent character and relate either to matters of public importance or to the arrangement of business, may be taken after a quarter to four o'clock, provided they have been submitted to the Speaker and have been accepted by him as satisfying the conditions imposed by standing order No. 7 and provided notice has been given to the minister concerned.
This is a very wise rule. Under the practice now followed here, a member may have shown his question to the minister concerned but he has kept it away from the Speaker, who, taken-
Rental Ceilings

by surprise, has no idea of the wording of the question and still is called upon to decide whether the question is in order or not. This is unfair to the Speaker, who is thereby placed in the same position as a judge called upon to render judgment without having seen the documents in the case. I venture to suggest that we accept the United Kingdom practice whereby the Speaker be shown beforehand any question to be addressed to ministers. Our procedure in this matter is hardly parliamentary. The time has arrived when it should be governed by practical rules.

subsubtopic: UPWARD ADJUSTMENT IN RENTAL CEILINGS OF COMMERCIAL ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the government has authorized certain amendments to the rental orders and regulations of the wartime prices and trade board. These amendments will permit an upward adjustment in rental ceilings of commercial accommodation and make provision by which this accommodation will gradually become free of controls. They will provide for the release from control of the prices of rooms in hotels and boarding houses in holiday resorts, and also provide certain relief for those who purchased tenanted houses as homes for themselves between November 1, 1944, and July 25, 1945.
More than a year ago, landlords and tenants of commercial accommodation were freed from rental controls if they were able to agree on a lease for a minimum term of five years with respect to premises then occupied by the tenant. Many landlords and tenants have made such leases and considerable commercial accommodation has already been thus released from control.
It has now been decided that another step along the road to complete decontrol of commercial accommodation can appropriately be taken. Accordingly a provision has been made that commercial accommodation will be released from rental control in cases where the landlord and tenant negotiate a lease for a minimum term of three years.
Rental control will be removed from commercial accommodation that is offered for rent for the first time, or that is now vacant or that hereafter becomes legally vacant, or which is wholly sublet.
The maximum authorized rental for all other commercial accommodation is increased by twenty-five per cent, provided that the landlord is prepared to enter into a lease for a minimum term of two years with the tenant. Such lease may be terminated by the tenant at any time on thirty days' notice but is binding on the landlord for the full two year term. If the tenant is not prepared to enter into such a lease at the increased rental, he may be required to vacate at the end of his present lease, and the accommodation will

Railway Act
thereafter be free from rental control. If the landlord is not prepared to offer such a lease to the tenant, the tenant may remain in occupancy after the expiration of his current lease as a tenant from month to month at the previous rental ceiling.
Accommodation in holiday resort hotels and holiday resort boarding houses is released from control. However, summer houses, tourist cabins and the like which, during the present housing shortage, are being used as permanent housing by non-transients will remain under control for the time being under the same regulations as other housing accommodation.
The only change which is being made in the present restrictions on eviction is in the case of a landlord who bought a tenanted house between November 1, 1944, and July 25, 1945. Such a landlord will be given an opportunity to prove to a court of rental appeals that he needs the house more than the tenant needs it; in which event he can give the tenant three months notice to vacate. This will provide relief for those who bought a tenanted house between these dates in the justifiable belief that they would be entitled to obtain occupancy of the house by serving notice on the tenant. This right was taken away by the "freezing of leases" order passed on July 25, 1945.

subtopic: PENSION BIGHTS-BREAKS IN SERVICE FROM CERTAIN CAUSES

speechtext:
Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 24, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, section 122(1)(c) of the Railway Act gives to railway boards of directors authority to establish retirement or pension plans. This bill would add to the appropriate paragraph thereof the following words:
Provided that in the administration of any railway retirement or pension plan, leave of absence, suspension, dismissal followed by reinstatement, a temporary lay-off on account of reduction of staff, or absence due to an industrial dispute, strike or lockout, shall not disqualify any railway employee from any retirement or pension rights or benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled.
The purpose of this amendment is to make it perfectly clear that the pension rights of railway employees, provided that such other conditions as are laid down in railway pension plans are met, cannot be lost or abrogated because of a break in service for any of the reasons indicated in the proviso which I have just read. This legislation, I regret to say, cannot be made retroactive to take care of the C.P.R. men involved in the 1919 strike, but it would prevent the recurrence of that kind of an injustice. That is the purpose of the amendment.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext: The house resumed from Frida3% February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West) for the second reading of Bill No. 18, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
In 1933 when the question of redistribution was under consideration I had the honour of being on the committee. I believe I am the only member of the present committee who served on the previous redistribution committee and therefore I feel some responsibility in assisting the gentlemen who are on the present committee in carrying on their labours.
When the minister introduced his bill I expected that he would give a number of rules and principles which the committee that is to be set up should follow. The bill itself contains nothing in the form of rules or principles. That is not the custom in the old country. In Great Britain in 1944, when the government brought in their bill to set up a commission to carry out redistribution, the Right Hon. Herbert Morrison, secretary for home affairs, did lay down a number of rules and principles to be followed by the commission. In other words the house did not propose to allow the commission to have all the say as to what it should do. The house itself, through the appropriate minister, gave certain directions.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit an interruption, I did mention the fact that our Prime Minister, in introducing a similar bill on a previous occasion, had gone into that question very throughly, and the matter is reported in a previous edition of Hansard. I did not think there was any need to go over the same ground again.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that it would have been better had he gone over the ground once more so as to refresh the memories of the members of the committee.
Redistribution

When Australia, New Zealand and South Africa set up their commission-and I may say that all these countries carry on their redistribution through a commission-they gave instructions regarding principles and rules. Since the situation in Australia is much like that in Canada, I will read, though not verbatim, the import of the rules in effect there.
(a)	That the committee give due regard to community interest or the diversity of community interest.
(b)	That the tradition and history of the ridings should also be taken into consideration.
(c)	That regard should be had to communications, such as railways and highways- and I presume we can now add aeroplane routes and water routes as well.
(d)	That the committee take into consideration the topographical characteristics of the ridings. They were to have regard to municipal boundaries as existing, as well as existing parliamentary boundaries and existing boundaries of the state ridings, Australia having several states corresponding to our provinces.
(f) That attention be given to the value of the vote in rural and urban communities respectively.
The basis of distribution in Australia comes down very largely to the basis of five, seven and nine. In other words, in a widely extended riding like West Algoma or Algoma, they would count five votes equivalent to nine votes in a city riding; or in a riding which was semi-city and semi-rural, like Oxford or Norfolk, for instance, they would count seven votes equivalent to nine votes in a large city riding. One of their previous acts pertaining to redistribution allowed a difference of twenty-five per cent above or below the quota. Their present act gives an allowance of twenty per cent above or below the quota. In New Zealand the limit was seven and a half per cent above or below the quota. Although I am not specifically speaking about the United States at the moment, I may say that in the United States the directions were ten per cent above or ten per cent below. In South Africa it is fifteen per cent above or fifteen per cent below; in Australia, twenty per cent above or twenty per cent below, and in Great Britain, twenty-five per cent above or twenty-five per cent below. I might say that those are only directions. There is a wide variation, as one will observe in studying the individual constituencies, in each one of those countries. I offer to this merely in order to show that the 'Mr. MaoNiflol.]
committee now being set up will at least have some other guide than the two directions which the minister gave.
As I started to say when I was speaking on Friday night, on the last occasion the late Hon. John Elliott and I-Mr. Elliott was chairman of the whole opposition committee and I was chairman of one-third of it, the Ontario section-established our own rules and regulations, and they were very largely those I have outlined. Of course, as any redistribution committee will find out, they cannot be followed exactly; so many factors have to be considered for and against. We did the best we could and, as I said previously, our final recommendations went through the house unanimously.
I look back with a certain amount of pleasure on what we did. We left thirty-two seats out of eighty-two wholly unchanged. We made eighteen seats out of full counties- that is, a full county made a seat; because one of the principles which is kept before any commission or committee is that of adhering as much as possible to county boundaries. In the United States more emphasis is laid on that principle than anywhere else I know of. In the United States no county is allowed to be cut in two. If a county has not sufficient population of its own, arrangements are made to take in another county with it. We can not wholly follow that here. I do not say that I am entirely in accord with it, because we have to make certain adjustments.
Four seats consisted of two counties each in Ontario. Two seats were a full county and part of a county, like the county represented by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who has the full county of Muskoka and the remainder of the county of Ontario outside of southern Ontario or Ontario seat. In no instance I believe did we make ridings out of three different counties. I am opposed to that. I can see a reason why you might cross from one county to another, but when you cross over three counties, that is going too far. Thirty-two seats were wholly within their counties. Seven seats were within the county and included a part of another county. Forty-six seats were within a spread of thirty-three and a third per cent above or thirty-three and a third per cent below the quota, which at that time, as you will remember, was 44,186. I admit that is not very close to the quota, but I think this committee will also find, when it gets into operation, that it will be difficult to get much closer to the quota than that in many cases. However, nineteen of the seats were over the quota, and seventeen under the quota beyond 33i per

neaistribution
cent. Thirty seats exceeded the quota and fourteen seats were within twenty per cent of the quota.
I have no apologies to make for anything we did. We did the best we could. I am satisfied we can defend every action we took.
I have always felt that it is the duty of a committee, particularly a parliamentary committee, to do the fair thing above everything else. Examination of the results of the several previous elections following redistribution will show that the government did not always win. It was not so the last time. I myself would not hesitate to go into any seat which has been called a gerrymander, but for which I was not responsible and do my best against whoever opposed me. I believe it is the opinion of the people of Canada generally, wherever they may live, that there should be fair play. That is the one thing they like above everything else. They resent having what they interpret as a gerrymander inflicted on them, and they generally resent being moved from one place to another.
I look forward to the committee doing its best, to see that nothing of the kind takes place in this redistribution. I have mentioned these rules, regulations and principles because I suppose every member of the house has heard certain rumours along the corridors as to what is to be done. I do not know that anyone really knows what is to be done in this redistribution, and I suppose the talk is just rumour. But I realize that the government must do certain things. There are some ridings which should be cut in two. The government's difficulty is going to be in finding the seats for what they want to do, because every time you disturb a seat you disturb half a dozen seats round about, unless you cut a county in two. Therefore I want to warn-perhaps I should not use the word "warn"; I suggest to members of the committee that they use their best judgment when it comes to eliminating seats in order to obtain the seats that are required to give necessary representation.
The riding of Nipissing has the largest population in Canada. I have always felt that anyone representing Nipissing during the last fifteen years should have had two or three indemnities, although they would likely have refused them; considering the work they have to do, they were entitled to them. I know that the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Gauthier) and his predecessor worked like Trojans from early morning to midnight; the correspondence they had to handle must have been tremendous. I believe the recent hon. member for Nipissing had more files in his
office than any other hon. member in the house, necessitated by the terrific amount of correspondence he had to handle. That is one seat which must be cut in two. When I say "must", I mean that I am very strongly in favour of cutting it in two. I know my word will not have any particular effect on the committee.

We are to have one extra seat in the province of Ontario and I would say that above everything else that seat should be given to Nipissing, the present population of which I suppose is closer to
125,000	than the 113,000 odd it had in 1941. Another very large seat is Ottawa West, but it has nothing like the right of Nipissing to another seat. In the one case, Nipissing covers a large area.

(Nipissing):	Better
people, too.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
But I say to my hon. friend it is right beside two or three radio stations; it has several newspapers and has other means of obtaining information which the county of Nipissing does not have. So when it comes to showing a preference between Ottawa and Nipissing, I say Nipissing should get that seat. Then certainly before Ottawa West has another seat the riding of Cochrane should be given consideration. It has a very large population; it covers an immense area; it takes in many gold mines, and I am sure the hon. member for that riding has worked night and day looking after his people. I believe the time is long past when this seat should have been divided. So far as I am concerned, seat No. 2 goes to Cochrane; but you have to find it first.
The county of Welland is the third largest in population. On the last occasion we did our best to give another seat that county, but we could not find one; so if Welland is to have
R edistribution

another seat this time it will be up to the government to find it somewhere else. There are others as well. I am told the county of York is to have another seat. We have fifteen constituencies there now, with a population of close to a million. I may be taking my own political life in my hands in saying this, but personally I am not going to be in favour of giving the county of York another seat on this occasion if it means wiping out a couple of other seats in Ontario. If seats must be found, it is the first duty of the committee to find them. Later, before I close, I am going to offer some advice in that regard.
Then I have heard rumours about putting certain counties together. I could deal with several of them, but I shall refer to only one. I heard that the riding of Muskoka-Ontario was to be added to two other ridings. Today that riding comprises the full county of Muskoka and the remainder of the county of Ontario not represented by the hon. member for Ontario. The constituency of Ontario has a population of some 52,000 at the present time, I believe, and takes in two or three townships in the county as well as Oshawa. I would be opposed to putting any more people in that riding. If you wipe out Muskoka-Ontario, where are you going to put it? I did hear some talk about putting that portion of the county of Ontario in the riding of Muskoka-Ontario into the constituency of Victoria, and Haliburton, but that now takes in two full counties; it is one of the largest ridings in Ontario, and it would be a monstrous thing if you added to it the largest portion of another whole county. Then I have heard it suggested that Muskoka be put in. with Parry Sound. That would be a monstrous thing, too. That would make Parry Sound the largest county in Ontario, with the exception of the northern counties. I say these things so that those planning what must be done may be warned of the position in regard to these matters.
I could go on to deal with a number of other constituencies which I hear are to be put together. Later I shall give my opinion as to what should be done in that regard, but right at the very beginning I wanted to state that in my 'humble judgment the riding of Nipissing has a better claim to the extra seat Ontario is going to get than any other constituency in this province, I do not believe many hon. members have made a more exhaustive study than I have made into election acts, systems of voting, redistribution and so on, not only for Canada but for all the British dominions. I have thoroughly

studied the situation in evrery riding in every British dominion, in addition to the redistribution acts that have been put through.
I see the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) looking at me. I might tell him I am not in favour of any change being made in his constituency. Middlesex county has three members including the city of London. It has been suggested that the two Middlesex ridings should be put 'together, but I can tell my hon. friend I shall oppose that move strenuously. It would not be fair at all. I can tell him further that on the last occasion his predecessor, Hon. John Elliott, and I agreed at 'the very beginning that Middlesex should not be altered.

speechtext:
I am going to support the amendment, too, a little later on. I said that Great Britain, Australia, South Africa and New Zealand have commissions. The other night someone asked the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) to whom the commissions reported and whether their reports could be changed. In New Zealand and South Africa the reports cannot be changed; it is sudden death down there. The proclamation is made by the governor general, I suppose on orders of ithe government, and there is no change. In Great Britain and Australia the report of t'he commission must come back to the house, where it is reviewed. If they are not satisfied it is sent back to the commission with their recommendations. So if a commission is set up here I would wish to feel that we were in the same boat as Great Britain and Australia. I would not want to surrender the right of this house to make any comment on the changes in seats; and I am sure that will not 'be done.
Before going further, while I yet have time,
I want to refer to what was said by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). This is an impossible seat, over 1,000 miles long by 750 miles wide, containing something less than 750,000 square miles. The Mackenzie area comprises

It should have been. I
do not want the minister to think I am finding fault. It is just a condition we are up against -and it is a difficult one. Here we have
750,000	square miles represented by one man.
I have been up there, over the ground. Starting at Forty Mile, down the Yukon river from Dawson, near the international boundary and going up the river one passes Dawson, McQuesten, Stewart, and off to one side there are Mayo and Keno. Then you go on up to Whitehorse and Carcross. That is about 750 miles, or a round trip of 1,500 miles.
Now we go to the other part of the proposed riding, Mackenzie district. Under ordinary circumstances one cannot fly across the mountains although, through the courtesy of the United States government, I had that privilege. A plane was put at my disposal when I was up there a couple of years ago. It was a very large plane, the largest I had seen up to that time, and one with power sufficient to go over those high mountains between Norman Wells and Whitehorse, a distance of 650 miles.
For the ordinary passenger plane to go to the Mackenzie district from the Yukon it would be necessary that it first go down to Nelson, 750 miles from Whitehorse, and then another 750 miles north to Norman Wells, and, over to Yellowknife. Or probably he would go over to Fort Smith, first. If he starts at Fort Smith, by plane, he would go to Resolution, on Great Slave, and from there to Providence, and from there to Simpson and from there to Wrigley, and from there to Norman, and next to Norman Wells, and next to Good Hope, and next to Arctic Red River, and then to McPherson and then to Aklavik.
That is over a thousand miles by plane, I went over it, and I know. I know how long it takes. And of course, I went by boat part of the way, too. Then, when one gets to Aklavik, it would be at least 500 miles to Coronation, where there is a settlement on Coronation gulf. Then he would go from there down to Rae on Great Slave lake. But first he would go from Coronation to Port Radium on Great Bear lake where, as the house knows, there is a substantial settlement, Then he
R edistribution

would go to Great Slave lake, and thence to \ ellowknife-and that is another thousand miles.
So I am going to say this to the minister, that in all fairness and justice if the amendment offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is defeated-as I expect it will be, although I am in favour of it-then in fairness to any candidates for the lukon, the nomination day should be four weeks in advance of the general election. It could not be done in anything less than that; it would keep anyone going for at least four weeks.
In addition to that, the official candidates should be provided at the cost of the government with commercial plane mileage and should be authorized a mileage of not less than 5,000, having in mind the mileages I have just placed before hon. members. Otherwise it would be impossible for any candidate to visit that gigantic area, which I believe is the second largest in the world. The only constituency which would be larger than the new Musk-Ox riding-if we call it ithat-^would be the constituency of Kalgoorlie in Australia. But there the conditions are wholly different; the climate is hot and the country is flat.
Our far north Musk-Ox constituency, comprising about 750,000 square miles, with" its two high ranges of mountains to overcome, would present gigantic problems. I believe in places the mountains to which I have referred are
6,000	feet high. When we were going over those mountains I was asked by those in charge of the aircraft if I wanted to wear a respirator. I said no, that I was strong enough to get along without it. It did not bother me, and I was certainly pleased to make the trip.
In fairness to any candidate the government may offer, and to the hon. member who now represents that constituency, and who has done so well and faithfully, for so many years, I make the plea that they be given the expense of an aeroplane. The same would apply to the candidate of any other party having ten seats in the house. It would be easy to prevent the use of that plane for anything other than government business. I make the plea in the belief that the measure will pass, and that the government's candidate and other candidates are entitled to British fair play, hnder present conditions a campaign to cover this area would be wholly impossible. After the election, once a year, or at least once in two years, the successful candidate should have the same privilege so that he might visit his constituency. Anyone who represents Yellowknife, Whitehorse and Dawson should be in a position to visit the territories. The country 
and parliament would expect the sitting member to do so, but it would not be possible without the use of a plane, free of charge. If necessary, I would ask the minister to introduce another bill to amend the elections act so that this plane expense could be shouldered by the government.
My concluding remarks will have reference to the amendment offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He is on sound ground, and on different occasions the Prime Minister has supported a similar suggestion. Every time he did so, advocating a commission, I gave him my support. My own leader and other leaders have advocated that the seats should be designated by a commission. I realize that this cannot be done now because we must work under the British North America Act.
If the amendment is defeated, then I appeal to the government either to extend the life of the committee after its work is through or set up a new committee, possibly to be called a Speaker's committee, the same as they did in England, which would make a careful survey- it will take possibly a year or two-of the workings of the commissions in the four countries of the commonwealth that now have commissions. That committee could then report back to this house.
No present member of the house would be affected in any way because nothing could be done until after the next election. No one will know what may happen several years hence when another election would be coming along. I suggest that the minister consider doing this after the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is defeated. I believe we are the only member of the commonwealth which does not redistribute its seats by a commission.
What do we find? Every member on the committee is importuned by those members whose seats are in jeopardy. I do not blame any hon. member for doing that. When anyone came to me I always treated him courteously and kindly; I treated him as I should have liked to be treated. A member cannot be blamed for trying to defend his seat; but that is not fair to the future candidates, it is not fair to the country, and it does not bring about a proper redistribution. If, as I know it will be, the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is defeated, then I advise the government to consider the proposal I have just made.
I recollect the last occasion I had a warm feeling for the Acting Speaker (Mr. Golding). It was proposed to eliminate his seat; but he is a working man; he has a thorough knowl-

edge of everything pertaining to industry and I said to myself, "If at all possible, that is the type of man we want in this house. We want more of them." So your own seat, Mr. Speaker, was saved by your good sense in approaching the committee in connection with it.
I heard the other day that an attempt was to be made to wipe out the seat of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell). This house should be proud of what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has done since he has been here. He has been an acquisition to the opposition and I know, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) were here at the moment, he would agree that he has been a great source of help to him in unravelling financial problems. I could hardly believe it when I heard that an attempt would be made to wipe out the hon. member's seat. If the seat is wiped out I know we shall have to try to get him another one, because this house cannot afford to be without the wisdom of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.
He represents a rural riding and, if you wipe out that riding to give another seat to York county, I am not in accord with that.
I have heard no request from Toronto or York county for a new seat. There are some small adjustments that perhaps could be made. The hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor) has a large constituency, almost as large as that of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). It is a larger constituency to cover because it consists of a populous suburban area and the large township of Markham. I quite agree that perhaps something could be taken off the riding of York East. That would be a simple thing to do. The township perhaps could be taken off and put in with York North, thus reducing the number of people in York East.
I appeal to the committee through the government to make as few changes as possible. There will be another census four years hence, after which there will be another redistribution. Perhaps in the meantime the government could set up a commission and then everything which was not adjusted this time could be adjusted. Why upset ridings everywhere just for four years? Why disturb the Acting Speaker's riding or the riding of the Deputy Speaker? I repeat that an effort should be made to have as few changes as possible. There are very few that really have to be made. I have looked over every seat in Ontario and very few of them need to be changed. Some could be reduced if necessary without injury to the rural seats. Let us set an example to the world by making as few changes as possible. That is why I said I
Redistribution
was not in favour of reducing the ridings in Middlesex county. Some say if necessary we could take some from Middlesex East and put them into Middlesex West, but I would advise to leave them alone. The hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) is a cattle man, and there are too few of them here. One of the best speeches I ever heard him make was on that subject.
I close with one further thought. If Carle-ton county is to have another seat it will mean taking another seat away from eastern Ontario, and I am opposed to that. As long as I am here I will be opposed to altering the Prime Minister's constituency of Glengarry. If that were altered it would affect the riding of the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand). One of the best speeches I ever heard the hon. member for Prescott make in this house was on the subject of cheese making. There would be a distinct loss if we reduced the number of seats in Ontario by combining Glengarry and Prescott. The riding of the hon. member for Prescott would thus be left out. To eliminate that riding would be a distinct loss to this house because the hon. member is one of the few members who knows all about cheese. There are too few men in this house who know about cheese making and cattle raising.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that in rising to speak on the second reading of the redistribution bill I am just a little bit confused over the wording of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It seems to me that if we dissect the amendment carefully and then read the speeches that have been made with respect to it we are bound to be confused as to the difference between the readjustment of representation and the readjustment of the electoral districts. I submit that there is all the difference in the world between the two, but the speeches which have been made do not indicate that.
The bill is an act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons and is based upon the constitutionality of the British North America Act. I take it that the bill is simply writing into the law that which already is basically the law as provided by the British North America Act. In other words, the British North America Act contains provisions which determine the number of representatives to be returned to the House of Commons from each province. That is one thing. But the readjustment of the boundaries of electoral districts is quite another thing. It seems to me-and I stand to be corrected if I am not right-that the amendment proposed by the
Redistribution

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might have more properly been proposed to the resolution standing on today's order paper in the name of the Secretary of State (Mr. Gibson). The difference is this. The resolution on the order paper is to refer the bill to a special committee, with instructions to prepare schedules. The bill itself, of course, is to have schedules attached to it. I fancy that what was in the mind of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in proposing his amendment was that the schedules should be given to an independent tribunal to prepare. I do not see the wisdom and I cannot see the use of having the readjustment of representation referred to a tribunal, because the readjustment is already provided for in the British North America Act. What could a tribunal do but sit around the table, take out their pencils, figure out the population of the different provinces according to the last census and then, according to the mathematical results obtained, declare that such and such a province is now entitled to so many representatives? That is all they could do. But if the hon. member had in mind a readjustment of the electoral districts I cannot see that I have a great deal to say against his proposal.

You may have a technical point there, but I claim I am right on that technicality. If the amendment carried, what we would be doing would be giving the right to an independent tribunal to come back to this house and recommend changes in the British North America Act. I know that is not the intention. If the resolution had read this way, "Resolved that in the opinion of this house the readjustment of electoral districts for representation in the House of Commons be referred to an independent commission," it would have made all the difference in the world.
After the amendment had been proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a government member or at least a member on the government side of the house I refer to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)-rose to answer him and stated that on one occasion that very thing was in the mind of the government. He referred to as far back as 1903 and went on to say that 
in 1939-and some of us remember it-a committee was set up to find out how other countries handled the redistribution of seats. The report referred to New Zealand, Australia, the United States, the Union of South Africa, so fourth and so on, and then the hon. member for Quebec South stated that on the basis of what those countries had done the government of that day saw considerable merit in referring the matter to a commission and was so impressed with the suggestions arising from the report that they decided to introduce a bill setting up a redistribution commission. In other words, the hon. member, speaking, I fancy, for the government, was making a good case for the amendment, but before he got through, of course he said that there were certain difficulties in the way with respect to the proposed bill. That bill was proposed but never introduced. If there were difficulties in the way it does seem to me that the government of that day must have known of those difficulties before they even proposed such a bill. I do not think that things have since changed in principle to give them any particular reason for changing their minds.
The hon. member on the government side then went on to say that the government, instead of introducing the measure, retraced their steps because one difficulty was to decide what instructions should be given to such a commission. The instructions that were proposed to be given to that commission appear on page 699 of Hansard. The commission was to give due consideration to:
(a)	The physical features;
That was referring to electoral districts.
(b)	Means of communication;
(c)	Existing boundaries of electoral districts, both provincial and federal;
(d)	Boundaries of administrative areas;
(e)	Such other pertinent factors as may occur to it or to which its attention may be drawn.
Those instructions are fairly explicit, although personally I think the last one, (e), leaves the thing pretty well wide open to the commission to do what they want. If there is any merit now in discussing the readjustment of electoral districts, I suggest that the body to which this task is entrusted, whether it be a special committee or, if the amendment carries, an independent tribunal, should divide the provinces into constituencies equal in population so far as possible, excepting, of course, that it is recognized that in cities and urban areas some allowance must be made in that respect.
The other matter which I think is more or less important is that the electoral district

Redistribution
should be in as complete a block as possible, and when I say "a block" I mean as square as possible, although I am not going to labour the square part of it. We know there are certain physiographical features that must be taken into consideration. There may be rivers. I do not know that that would apply so much in Ontario as in some districts of the far north where there are huge rivers and very few bridges. In some instances geographical features have to be considered, but that is not true of any great number of constituencies; it applies to a comparative few.
What we have to get away from is the tendency toward gerrymandering things around to gain some political advantage. That is, because one particular district voted a certain way in the last election, therefore it should be included here or there in order to give the government of the day a certain support. That is a thing we have to get away from, and that is the thing which I fancy has happened in the past.
I do not know the description of all the electoral districts in Canada but I have in mind one in the province of Alberta. Take, for instance, the constituency of Calgary East.
The fact of the matter is that it is not in east Calgary at all. It takes a slice of two or three blocks clean through the centre of the city of Calgary and then toward the south it takes in a lot of rural territory. East Calgary proper is in the constituency of Bow River. Surely there must have been some gerrymandering to bring that about, and so I say that is the tiling we have to get away from.
In this respect may I suggest that while, of course, railroads and highways have something to do with the facilities of travel of members in their constituencies, we are living in a day that is remote from the horse and buggy age. I believe most members travel by automobile. There are a few constituencies -Peace River, Cariboo and some of those ridings-where you have to fly or wade through mud or something of that sort, but such constituencies are not large in number, and I think they should be made as much as possible in a complete, well-rounded or square block, although, as I said before, I shall not labour the square part of it.
As regards gerrymandering, there is, of course, no guarantee that an independent tribunal would not do the same thing. They could do as much of that as a committee of the house could. Another matter is this. I do not quite know what may be meant by 'independent tribunal". That is a term that would have to be defined. One might say that a judicial committee is independent. I
do not know; perhaps it is. I should like to think it is or that it would be, and I believe that, if anything, it should be, because it is composed, for the most part, of judges chosen from the judiciary of the country. But there is no guarantee that they would not do some gerrymandering just the same, and so I think we need to define the term and to say what we mean by "independent tribunal."
If by "an independent tribunal" is meant a tribunal composed of men designated by the various political parties in the country, the only fair thing to do would be to give the biggest party the biggest slice of the personnel on the committee, and there is no guarantee that such a committee would not do some gerrymandering.
The hon. member for Quebec South, speaking against the amendment, said that another feature which caused the government of some years ago not to introduce their bill was that such an independent tribunal would eventually have to report to parliament, and what would we do with their report? Of course the same is true now even under a parliamentary committee, because you have to adopt their report. That has to be done in any event. But that, to my mind, was the best argument he had, although even that argument must have occurred to the government of some years ago before they ever thought of bringing down a bill at all.
That argument is one which I would classify as a choice between democracy and bureaucracy, and that, to my mind, is the principal test in connection with a vote on the amendment. I see in the amendment a tendency *toward putting the thing in the hands of bureaucrats, and I must say I am pleased that the hon. member for Quebec South looked at the matter with a view to making democracy a little more effective. If he can be as persuasive with his own government in all that they do in that regard, perhaps we shall be more satisfied; for the country in the past few years has certainly been run by the bureaucrats. We want to get away from that, and the truth of the matter is that this is a piece of legislation applying to the House of Commons, which is the business of the House of Commons, and it should be the right of members of the house to determine it. With that principle in mind, I am afraid I shall have to vote against the amendment.
There is one other point I would bring out. The committee that is eventually to be set up will be one composed of twenty-five members. I believe that, in the allocation of these members among the various parties, the Liberal party will have fourteen members and

the combined opposition, eleven. This means that the government party will have three members to the good.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said some of the things I would have said, but I cannot agree with him in his general conclusion. One thing I think the emphasis should be put on is that the readjustment of the electoral districts in this country is perhaps of more concern to the people themselves than to the members of parliament who represent those people; because members of parliament, efficient, good and honest as they may be, are bound to be prejudiced by the position in which they find themselves.
I thought the speech of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) was probably one of the best arguments that could be advanced for the amendment proposed by my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I can see that in a committee appointed from the members of the House of Commons there would be an entering into of interminable arguments about Bruce county, for instance, or some other county and the boundaries which should be fixed, particularly as it would affect the fate of certain members, either friends or enemies on the respective sides of the house. In a committee of that kind I think there would even be what they call political wrangling and horse trading of all kinds. That is the opinion which I think is held by many of the electors of this country to whom I have referred.
I have not had a long experience in this house, but I have some experience of what the

people outside the house talk about. They say that there would be political juggling, with every man playing his own hand. It has been hinted, of course, that any committee which is chosen from among the members of this house would have a predominance of votes from the government side; that a government man would be the chairman and that on that committee there would be a majority of votes on the government side. I am making no accusations; I am stating that merely as a fact. Some people have mentioned the word "gerrymander". I do not suppose that either I or the people of Saskatchewan are the only ones who have that idea. For instance, I was noticing that some people in Quebec have the same opinion, because I see that our new colleague, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette), used the following words. I hope hon. members across the way will forgive my French. I speak with good intentions, even though with poor pronunciation :
(Translation):
Mr. Knight:	Some would even lead us to
believe that the government might even exert their influence or their power to operate a redistribution in favour of the Liberal party.
(Text):
I notice that hon. gentlemen did not applaud either my pronunciation or the sentiment expressed in that sentence. .
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said that the fate of this amendment in his mind-and perhaps as to his vote-depends somewhat on the meaning of the word "independent". When one mentions an independent committee in this country, one somehow thinks of a judicial committee or a committee headed by a judge. We have already had a statement made in this house, although, I forget which hon. member made it, that perhaps even judges have their prejudices. So far as I am concerned, I do not see the necessity for having a judge on such a committee. This is a matter of geography. It is a matter of numbers of people. It is a matter of statistics. I see no reason why we could not have statisticians and' geographers on that committee-and them only, if you like- and have the thing fixed on a scientific basis.
I do not think the members of the committee should be people who are implicated and whose political careers depend upon the results of the decision of. such a committee.
There was mentioned here the other day another matter to which I am violently opposed. I do not believe that any consideration should be given to any member of this house, whether he be a leader of a political party, such as the Prime Minister (Mr. FEBRUARY 24, 1947
Redistribution
Mackenzie King) or anyone else. I have the greatest respect, in many ways, for our Prime Minister; and I certainly have the greatest respect for my own leader. But I do not think either one of them is entitled to any consideration such as one often hears, "Oh, that is So-and-so's seat; we must do this or we must do that." I do not think any member of this house should have any consideration whatever in that regard. The moment this parliament is dissolved, every hon. member ceases to have any vested interest in the particular seat which he has occupied.
As I said before-and this is the thought I wish to leave with the house as I sit down- redistribution should be out of the hands of those who are implicated or who are personally concerned in the result. I think a scientific committee such as I have suggested would be independent. It could be chosen from men who have never shown any disposition for any particular activity in politics. I think this principle of impartiality is vital. So far as we in this party are concerned, we believe in hewing to the line of fairness; let the chips fall where they may. In any scheme of distribution we believe that the principle of impartiality must be preserved.
Mr. II. G. ARCHIBALD (Skeena): Mr. Speaker, I should just like to bring out a few points which to some extent apply to my own position and the position of .some of the other northern members. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) the other evening brought out the position of one who is a member representing a vast area. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) mentioned the fact that air services should be put at the disposal of members in given ridings, to which suggestion I heartily agree. Take, for instance, Atlin, which lies just below Whitehorse and is in the riding of Skeena. That has more community of interest with Yukon than it has with British Columbia; yet, owing to the British North America Act it must remain part of the Skeena ridiing. The hon. member for Yukon pointed out that the riding should be projected into the north country rather than taking the Mackenzie district right across Canada. Preserve me from being any closer to the north pole than I am right here in Ottawa.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the government the fact that science is eliminating time and space with modern instruments such as air transportation, while the pass of the ordinary member is not good for this type of travel. In the case of a member who can prove that he cannot get into an area by any other method than air transportation, I believe such transportation
should be supplied, because these people are not getting the services of their members. I should like to see the government take up this matter and solve the difficulty in some way.

No; I am just speaking on the amendment. Several hon. members have spoken in support of the proposal that we have an independent commission, and the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) spoke of the necessity of having an impartial committee. But the hon. members have not suggested how we may be assured that a committee or all its members will be impartial, nor have they suggested a test of impartiality. It has been suggested from time to time that supreme court judges should be appointed on such a commission; it has been felt that because they are outside politics and do not vote-which I understand is at their own request-they should be qualified to form such a commission.
One of the objections I see to the proposal that we have an outside commission deal with the matter is that the report of such a commission must come back to the house. When a bill is referred to a committee consisting of members of the house, that committee reports to the house and its members can be present to give their reasons for arriving at the conclusions contained in the report. An independent commission composed of men who were not members of the House of Commons would submit a report to this house, and it would be debated without having them present to give any explanation as to how or why they arrived at the conclusions they reached. It is very much for that reason, as well as for the reasons given by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when this matter was discussed last week, concerning the difficulty of giving instructions to such a commission, that it was felt the bill should be brought forward in the same form as in previous years.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Before this amendment is put, I should: like to say a few words in support of the principle involved. The question of what would constitute an independent commission was raised by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han-sell) and, greatly to my surprise, by the minister in charge of the bill. I say "greatly to my surprise" because almost every day the
Redistribution

government is appointing commissions that at least are supposed to be independent; and I supposed that this commission, if it were appointed, would be created in the same way and would be considered an independent commission. I imagine, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested that a commission was a better way of dealing with this question than a parliamentary committee, he felt sure that an independent commission could be set up.
What do we consider constitutes independence when we are dealing with a question of this kind? We are thinking of persons who are not interested from a personal point of view in the particular question with which they have to deal. That being the case, I am convinced that we could choose a commission of three or five, or whatever number may be required-I think perhaps three would be sufficient-who would be independent from that point of view.
Another point raised by the minister was that the report of this commission would have to come before parliament and that there would be no one here from the commission to explain it to the members of the house. Well, my understanding of such commissions' reports is that the explanation or reason for the action taken or the recommendations made forms part of the report, and if members of parliament are not sufficiently intelligent to understand those reasons, obviously they should not be here. In Great Britain, where a commission decides such matters, the report of the commission is presented to parliament, and I have never heard of the British parliament having any difficulty in coming to a decision in adopting such reports.
The purpose of the redistribution bill is to rearrange or redefine the boundaries of constituencies because of changes in population that have taken place since the last census, and, on this occasion, because of the changes made at the last session of parliament through amendments to the British North America Act. The proposal of the government is that a parliamentary committee be appointed to redefine the boundaries of the constituencies, and my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has moved an amendment stating that in the opinion of this house a commission would be a better way of doing that work. I think there can be no doubt as to the correctness of the principle contained in the amendment. As the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) has said, defining or delineating the boundaries of constituencies is a scientific and technical matter, not a political question at [Mr. Maclnnis.l
all; at least it should not be a poltical question. After all, members come and members go but the electors remain in these constituencies, and it is their interests that should be served. It has been suggested by some and implied by others that the sitting member should be consulted before changes are made in the boundary of his constituency. That suggestion presupposes that the sitting member has a vested interest in the constituency. When the committee meets it will be something like a miniature league of nations, with each member being the shah or the fuehrer or the emperor of this or that constituency and horse-trading with the other members of the committee to protect his interests. May I remind hon. members that this measure does not come into effect, except for the appointment of returning officers, until parliament is dissolved. Section 8 states:
This act shall take effect only upon the dissolution of the present parliament:	Provided
that for the purpose only of authorizing and enabling the appointment, pursuant to section eight of the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, of returning officers, whenever required, this act shall be deemed to be in force on the date upon which it has been assented to.
But it does not come into effect until the dissolution of parliament; and when parliament is dissolved there are no sitting members. They may still cluck but they do not sit. We must keep in mind that, if the sitting member has an interest here, so have the candidates already nominated or who may be nominated in any particular riding. So let us get away from the idea that we have a vested interest in our constituencies. If there were anything needed to convince me as to the desirability of this proposal, it would be the speech made by my good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I am not reflecting upon the hon. member at all. I believe we both arrived in the house at the same time, in 1930, and in the main we have been good friends ever since. Indeed, since he came to this side of the house we have been more friendly than we used to be when he sat on the other side of the house and tried to defend a government which could not be defended.

Mr. Speaker, the only thing I wish to say on this motion is that I want to register my objection to the way in which it is proposed to set up this committee, because no provision has been made for the representation of an important element of the population. There are in this house sixty-four members from the province of Quebec, of whom fifty-six are Liberals, leaving eight members outside that party.
It has always been the custom, in the setting up of such a committee, to have, as far as possible, representations of all the elements of the population. We have on this side of the house six members from the province of Quebec who are not recognized officially as a distinctive group; nevertheless I can state that we represent not only six constituencies but many hundred of thousands of voters, taking into consideration the number of votes that were given to the Independent and Bloc Populaire candidates in the 1945 election.
My contention is that the way in which the redistribution committee is set up creates grave injustice to those hundreds of thousands of voters who are not represented on it. The government has stated in many instances that there shall be no gerrymandering in the next redistribution but I am afraid that, if things are left as they now are, there is great danger of such gerrymandering. Therefore it is my duty, before it is too late to request of the government that this motion be amended so that the members to whom I have just referred may be adequately represented. It would be very easy for the government to ask these six members to designate one of them to be on the committee and, if the minister would postpone the motion until tomorrow, we would be able to let him know whom we wanted to have as the representative of those six members.

The remarks just made by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) cannot be allowed to pass without comment. The hon. member has stated that of the sixty-four members from the province of Quebec fifty-six are Liberals While eight are not. For the fifty-six Liberals there axe five members

Redistribution
on the committee and for the eight others the leader of the opposition, or the opposition, has chosen one. 1 think that is fair. The representative of those eight is neither an Independent nor a Bloc Populaire, but it cannot be said that this is the fault of the government because, after all, the whips suggest the names of the members of the different parties and it is up to the authorities in the opposition to designate the member they choose. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) was designated, a member in whom I have, and I am convinced my colleague has, great confidence. It can never be said that the hon. member for Stanstead, even if a Conservative, has any racial prejudice.
If my hon. friend the member for Charle-voix-Saguenay is not on the committee; if none of his five friends is on the committee, he cannot 'hold that against the government, because it would be surprising if the Liberal party undertook to name someone to represent the hon. gentleman and his friends on the committee when the hon. gentleman and his friends have not any confidence in the Liberal party.
My hon. friend should blame the opposition, with whom he and his friends have consistently voted and to whom they have given their confidence in the past. Indeed, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has had such complete confidence in the party opposite that he was chief organizer for the Conservatives in the district of Quebec.
In the old days.

In the old days? In 1932, when the friends of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay were in power, when the Conservatives, whose organizer he was in the district of Quebec, were in power, what happened so far as the committee on redistribution set up at that time was concerned? There were then twenty members on the committee: Thirteen Conservatives, six Liberals and one'Labour. Of the thirteen Conservatives there were two Canadians of French descent; the others were not. Of the six Liberals there were two of French descent; one was from the province of Quebec and the other represented the French minorities of other provinces.
Where was justice at that time-with the Liberal party or the Conservative party? Today, justice for minorities is found in the Liberal government again. Of the twenty-five members of the committee, eight members-and they are all Liberals-are of French descent, or one-third. Five represent the province of Quebec, while three represent the minorities in the other provinces. Where was 83166-47J
justice in 1932? Was justice given by the Liberal party, or was justice given by the party for whom my hon. friend was chief organizer at the time in Quebec?
Moreover, not only is justice done to minorities on this occasion ; it is done to all parties, as one hon. member on the other side said this afternoon. I see no reason for complaint or for the fear that there will be any gerrymandering. If there was gerrymandering, it was in 1932 when the counties in the province of Quebec were cut up with a view to electing Conservatives in 1935. Such a thing, I am convinced, will not happen this time.

There are one or two remarks I should like to make on this motion. In the first place, I wish to support what was said by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) in discussing this bill on redistribution the other evening. His complaints were, in my opinion, quite justified.
With regard to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in connection with the amendment, the hon. member said:
. . . the rural constituencies . . . varied all the way from Souris with a population of 25,000 to Selkirk with a population of 52,000. Similarly in Ontario the variation in rural constituencies ran all the way from 18,000 for the constituency of Glengarry to 88,000 for the constituency of Nipissing.
I have also found it very interesting to notice that a number of constituencies which seemed to have been traditionally Tory, at the time of the last redistribution, were carved out in such a way as to include a rather small population.
I just wanted to refer to this because recently a couple of editorials have appeared in the Winnipeg papers about the constituency of Souris being traditionally Tory. I am very happy to say that over the years from 1903 to 1940 the electors have divided their votes politically fifty-fifty between Liberals and Conservatives.

man.

I just wish to say
that I was rather confused about how I might have voted on the amendment proposed by the hon. member, especially in view of the fact that my name was proposed as a member of this committee. I do not look forward to membership on this committee with any great deal of pleasure. I never had any such experience before. I should have liked a more independent committee to deal with this matter. I am one of those who, during the war years, became very much fed-up with controls and bureaucracy.

But you want to appoint another committee.

I am opposed to
appointing the suggested independent committee, and on that very principle, that it seems like the continuation of more bureaucracy and more controls, something to which I am very much opposed. I have never yet refused a challenge, or to do my duty as I saw it. As I say, I do not look forward with pleasure to being a member of this committee, but I think it is a challenge.
I listened intently to the various arguments advanced with respect to this measure. While we are members of the House of Commons, I think it is our duty to deal with these measures, and that is why I voted as I did for the government measure. As a member of this committee I may say that, as far as I am concerned, there will be no attempt whatsoever at gerrymandering. As far as I am concerned and, I think, as far as the speaker who has just taken his seat is concerned, we shall do a job on this on a fair basis. As far as I am concerned, it will be done along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) this afternoon, the chief thought being as to population and geography. We shall give a great deal of thought and attention to this and do the best we can along these lines.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks, like those of the other hon. members who have just spoken, will also be brief. In setting up this committee, however, I believe we might give some thought to some formula which they might go on. In introducing the redistribution bill the other night, the Secretary of State (Mr. Gibson) explained, as most of us were aware, that the quotient to be applied will be 45,556. I think all of us are agreed that, as far as it is practical, the constituencies should come fairly close to that quotient. We also have to bear in mind, of course, that there are some areas of Canada where the population is very sparse; and if a member is to serve his constituency as I believe he should be able to serve it, he should have an area which will allow him to visit his constituents. An area perhaps up to 5,000 square miles might be reasonably well covered once a year, but if it is any larger than that it will certainly be very difficult to cover it. I think the committee should be under some instruction to attempt to boost the population of the small constituencies so that constituencies very large in area and very large in population may be reduced.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) this afternoon stated that, as far as he was concerned, he hoped the Ontario seats might be left somewhat the same as they are. He stated that it had been brought to his attention that the seat of Muskoka-Ontario might be one of those which fell by the wayside, and he hoped the hon. member would be allowed to retain that seat because he had made valuable contributions to this house. With that I agree, especially for this reason, that the population of that constituency is 35,285, and I do not think it is exceedingly small. I think the committee, in bringing in its recommendations, should try to divide up this nation into electoral divisions of a size and character which will allow the people to be truly represented and truly to have a voice in parliament.
I am thinking now of the constituency of Glengarry which has a population of 18,732. At the same time I am thinking of the constituency of Nipissing with a population of 113,866. Surely by no stretching of an argument can it be said that the people of Nipissing are adequately represented in this house. Their population is almost two and a half times the quotient that is provided. I think this committee should be very careful that Canada does not get into the state of having a bunch of pocket boroughs.
I have done some calculating here on the basis of the constituency of Glengarry. If the eight provinces, with the exception of Prince Edward Island and Yukon, had their population divided amongst 242 seats, at 18,700 per seat, that would give a total population of
4,525,000	and the remaining eight seats could then have a population of 6,866,199. I do not think such a report will come from this committee. But we should realize that this committee can bring in any report it wishes, and some consideration should be given to seeing that a proper report is brought in.
The argument used by the Secretary of State that the rural population should have a greater proportionate representation in this house on the basis of population is also a good one. He enumerated what I considered were valid reasons but I do not intend to repeat them.
I have a proposition to lay before the house which I think would help the committee in adjusting the rural seats. It would mean that certain rural constituencies should be expanded, quite a number of them; and I do not wish the house to come to the conclusion that I am advocating that rural representation be reduced because, while some of the rural

Redistribution
constituencies are very small, some others are also very large and certainly they should be evened up as much as possible.
I am going to suggest that no constituency should have a population of less than 30,000 if at the. same time it has an area of less than
5,000	square miles. If the committee would apply such a formula, it would mean no change in British Columbia, which has three seats with less than 30,000 population; Kamloops, Kootenay East and Skeena, the areas of which are all over 16,000 square miles, and the constituency of Skeena having an area of 152,474 square miles. If this formula were applied, it would make no difference in Alberta, which has only one; seat with a population of less than 30,000, namely Acadia, and its area is over 10,000 square miles. It would make no difference in the basis of the representation for Saskatchewan, because that province has no constituencies with a population of less than 30,000. As far as New Brunswick is concerned, there is one constituency, namely Charlotte, with a population of 22,728, and an area of 1,290 square miles. This constituency I think should be increased by one-third in population, and that might well be used to decrease the population of the constituency of York-Sunbury, which has a population of 44,743 and an area of 4,700 square miles.
In Nova Scotia, there is one constituency, namely Antigonish-Guysborough, with a population of 26,006 and an area of 2,180 square miles. Also, in that province, there is the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings, with a population of 57.604 and an area of 2,790 square miles. So that one constituency here, namely the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough, should, I believe be enlarged to give it a population of at least 30.000, which would help reduce the area and population of one of the other larger constituencies.
Coming to the province of Quebec, I find three constituencies with a population of less than 30,000, and each of these three has an area of less than 900 square miles. But, as has been mentioned here this evening, the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay has a population of 67,087 and an area of 385,000 square miles. In other words, its population is more than twice as large as any of the three constituencies I have mentioned, and its area at least fifty times as great. There are also the constituencies of Chapleau and Lake St. John, with areas of 78,800 and 23,950 miles, respectively, and fairly large populations. The constituency of Pontiac is large and, I believe, should be reduced.
Coming now to the last province with which I wish to deal, Ontario, I would not wish to
accuse any political party of gerrymandering, but certainly it is odd to see some of the constituencies in that province, and the population and area of those constituencies. In Ontario there are seventeen seats with populations less than 30,000, and of those, sixteen are less than 5,000 square miles in area. The constituency of Glengarry is the smallest. These sixteen seats have each a population of less than 30,000, while on the other hand the constituency of Port Arthur has a population of 50,833 and an area of 140,800 square miles. The constituency of Cochrane has a population of 81,112 and an area of 72,000 square miles. The constituency of Kenora-Rainy River has a population of 47,743 and an area of 52,200 square miles. Finally, Nipissing has a population of 113,866 and an area of 10,000 square miles. If you add the populations of those sixteen small constituencies and the four large ones you get a total of 800,000, which would give an average population of about
40,000	and an average area of 14,645 square miles. With sixteen constituencies each having an area of less than 5,000 square miles and four constituencies having an area of 10,000 square miles or more, certainly there is room for improvement without reducing the representation from the rural areas. I have totalled the population of the constituencies of Glengarry, Brant, Huron-Perth, Middlesex West and Haldimand, and I get a total population of 107,000. So that the total population of these five constituencies is 6,000 less than that of one constituency in Ontario, Nipissing, while the area of those constituencies totals just a little more than twenty-five per cent of the area of the constituency of Nipissing.
Because I believe the committee should be given some direct instruction, I move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):
' That the motion be amended by inserting after the word "Commons" in the fourth and fifth line thereof the following words:
"provided that with the exception of the electoral divisions of the province of Prince Edward Island, no electoral division described in said schedules shall contain less than 30,000 population according to the decennial census of 1944, except in the case of electoral divisions with an area of more than 5,000 square miles."
I believe that amendment is reasonable. Surely this house has power to recommend a formula for the guidance of the committee. If such an amendment were carried, the people of this country would be more truly represented in the House of Commons.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following the remarks of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) as to the method of dealing with the matter now before us, there is something to which I wish to direct his attention. The hon. member stated his belief that this was the best way to deal with this matter in keeping with our responsibilities as a parliamentary democracy. I should like to refer him to the House of Commons redistribution of seats act, 1944, of the United Kingdom. I would direct attention to the fact that this act was passed by the United Kingdom parliament during the previous administration, and that it sets up permanent boundary commissions to deal with these matters.
