Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 23, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.
Just a moment, Mr. Speaker. I should like to say a word-
Are we not to have a statement from the minister on a bill of this importance?
Am I in order, Mr. Speaker? Have I the floor?
Order.

I rise to a point of order. The leader of our party has asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether, in view of the importance of this bill, he is prepared to make a statement. Surely our leader is entitled to an answer from the minister.
Order. I put the motion of the minister for the second reading of this bill. The hon. member who has the floor rose, and I saw him first, so he may proceed.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long.
Hear, hear.

But if there are many more bursts of applause like that, I shall take my full forty minutes. I just wish to refer to this bill as another of those belated but necessary steps in the long struggle that the producers of this country have had in their endeavour to get orderly marketing. It has been the belief of the organized producers of western Canada, anyway, and, I believe, of most of Canada, that we must have orderly marketing in the sale of our farm products if we are ever to have those products exchanged at a figure that will give the consumer of those products the necessary food supplied at prices he can pay.
It has been a long struggle. We started many years ago, before many hon. members now in the House of Commons were born. Many of the older ones were quite young at the time. There were the old Grangers; then the territorial grain growers' association, and then the older members will remember all those various steps which took place, leading up to the formation of the pools.
With the coming of the pools there came a conscious realization of the part the organized farmers have played; and the realization by those farmers that their safety, security and well-being depended upon the ability of the consumer to use their products. This means a fair price to the farmer and prices to the consumer that he can pay.
To achieve this end, organized agriculture recognized that all unnecessary transactions in marketing must be eliminated, and that production costs must be kept to a minimum. Now, to support that statement, and to lead up to the point I wish to get at as I go along, I should like to quote from the handbook of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, printed in 1924, and setting out the aims and objectives of the wheat pools of western Canada. These aims and objectives are as follows:
To reduce manipulation, speculation and waste, and any unnecessary transactions in the marketing of wheat;
To increase consumption, build up new markets and develop new uses for grain;
To market same directly and with regularity, so as to furnish it economically to the users thereof, and
To preserve for the grower and the public their proper profits and economies.
Regardless of all the obstacles they have met, and the set-backs with which they have been confronted from time to time, they have not altered these basic principles. As evidence of that, I shall quote from a statement

Canadian Wheat Board Act
by Mr. A. F. Sproule, first vice-president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, in his "Review of Pool Objectives" since 1924. He made this review in 1946, less than a year ago:
1.	To ensure for the producer of wheat adequate prices, orderly marketing of the crop and efficient handling services, in short, stability and a fair standard of living;
2.	To ensure to the consumer of wheat that he receives his supplies regularly, at reasonable prices, whether in times of plenty or scarcity, and at prices which, while giving the farmer a fair living, are not swelled by excessive costs of handling and distribution.
That is the same principle in 1946 as was announced in the year of the birth of the pools. This should dispel any ideas which some hon. members may have that the farmers wish to extract the last cent from the consumer when he, the consumer, is over a barrel, as he is at present, and, conversely, be exposed to retaliation by the consumer when the farmer may be occupying that unenviable position.
International coordination of marketing and international cooperation have been the consistent aim of the organized growers of this country. They were instrumental in calling a marketing conference in 1926 in St. Paul, Minnesota, and another in Kansas City in the following year. They gave active leadership in the two-day conference of representatives of producers' marketing organizations from all over the Dominion of Canada during the world grain exhibition and conference held at Regina in 1933.
The pools took an active part in promoting the empire producers conference held at Sydney, Australia, in March and April, 1938, and sent representatives to that conference; and I could give countless illustrations of the determined efforts of the farm organizations to have orderly marketing introduced.
They have pressed constantly for a Canadian grain board to market in an orderly way our cereal crops. During the 1930's, in the days of depression, the farmers were well aware that grain surpluses were not the result of over-production, but that they were the direct result of underconsumption-poverty in the midst of plenty-and they tried to arouse the public and the government of the day to a realization of that situation. They were eventually successful in persuading a reluctant Tory government to create the Canadian wheat board in 1935, when a Liberal opposition did their utmost-
You have no more adjectives, have you?
-and were ultimately successful, partly to emasculate the proposed act of that time. Replying to the hon. member, I have plenty of adjectives.
Give them to us, then.

If the hon. member would like me to reel off some adjectives applicable to himself, I would be quite capable of doing so; but the rules of the house would not permit me to use the ones I should like to.
After years of constant struggle, organized agriculture was successful in persuading an equally reluctant Liberal government to improve the act and to improve marketing arrangements and agreements to a limited extent.
The desire of organized agriculture to cooperate with consumers, to the end that all should be served equitably, was refused recognition by capitalist dominated governments, until the recent world war broke out; and it took two great statesmen, meeting in mid-Atlantic, to agree and announce that, if a permanent peace were ever to be achieved, then freedom from want was a cardinal requisite.
Since then, men of good will from over forty nations met at Hot Springs, Virginia, and, after discussion, announced in practical terms the practical methods which would need to be employed if the people of the world, who had never had enough to eat, were to be lifted out of that terrible position. The united nations relief and rehabilitation association showed a most practical application of those methods in the distribution of food to needy people; and it is a great pity that the United States decided to kill that organization.
In my opinion, a synchronization of the machinery of Canada and the United States for the production, processing and distribution of food stuffs would have led the world farther toward peace and good will than standardization of their military equipment will ever do.
The justice of the farmer's contention, that both he and the consumer of his products are of equal importance, is being recognized at high levels of administration today; and that recognition is apparent in the present wheat agreement with Britain, in the much hoped for international agreements, to be discussed at the conference in March, and in this bill. Suggestions for that conference are contained in the appendix to Votes and Proceedings of February 18, for this session of parliament.
If our Tory friends would devote more of their energies to promotion of such worthwhile projects, and less to military preparedness they would serve the cause of world peace much better; and the same can be said cf many Liberals in the house.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

We agree with the principle of this bill and see no valid reason for its passage being delayed by being referred to the agriculture committee. Every member of the house has heard the pros and cons discussed in newspapers, on the radio, on the platform and in conversation, and every member should by now have made up his mind on the principle. We believe that discussion of this bill should be confined to the committee of the whole in this chamber, where every member who has a conviction can, and should, place himself on record for the country and the world to see and judge.
We agree in the wisdom of creating the wheat board. We reserve the right to examine and criticize its operations. This can and should be done by a parliamentary committee. We agree in the wisdom of envisaging long-term contracts with one or more nations willing to enter into such agreements. We are not in full agreement with the domestic policy which is at present a corollary of the agreement with Britain. We sincerely hope that the forthcoming conference in March will result in international agreements which can and, we believe, will, do more than any other single thing to create international good will. Let me point out here that I am not congratulating the Tories for creating the wheat board, even though we wanted it, nor am I congratulating this Liberal government for some improvements in its operations during the past three years or for the amendments offered in this bill. We are in agreement with the principles contained in the act and in this bill, even though we shall offer some advice and possibly some amendments to certain clauses in the bill.
My congratulations are to those thoughtful and cooperatively minded farmers and their elected officers for the partly successful results of their constant and steady pressure to have enactments of this sort. They had to overcome great reluctance on the part of both Liberals and Tories to gain even this much ground. Let me tell this house further that, while the great farm organizations of Canada do not espouse any political party, the membership, who are free to support any party they like, have come to realize that they must fight their battles against speculation in the product of their labour and against monopoly exploitation on the political as well as on the economic front. That is one of the reasons why Saskatchewan has practically eliminated the Liberal and Tory parties.

And all freedom too.
MR. BENTLEY: There is more freedom there today than we ever had under the

Tory regime. The membership realize that only a party sympathetic to their desires and understanding their needs can carry their demands to parliament.
There have been those in this house, and outside, who have said that the organized farmers have failed in the past. Let me state here that they have not failed. They have met obstacles, but have steadily removed them; they have suffered reverses, but have remained undismayed; they have pressed steadily on toward their objective, and will continue to do so, because they believe in the justice of their goal and they never lie down on the job or turn back.
Let me remind the house of what I said at the beginning of my speech. This bill is only a step, one of a few that have been taken hesitantly by this and past governments, one of many that will have to be taken much more rapidly and more generously by governments in the future. We will support the principle and insist that it carry out its proper purpose, namely, eliminate speculation, manipulation and waste, and all unnecessary transactions in marketing, and preserve for the producer and consumer fair and just relationship in the exchange of the products of the labour of each.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that this bill provides a basis upon which a sound grain policy can be built, a policy which will be in the interests of both the producer and the consumer. Let me say to the minister that, before we can support the second reading of this bill, we must have assurance that when we reach the committee stage he will either move an amendment or accept an amendment to commit the government to accepting all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950. I believe that it is the intention of the government to accept delivery of all wheat for which they have room, but that is not what the bill says. The bill merely commits the government to taking delivery of a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre on a specified acreage.
The specified acreage is outlined by the board and in many cases it will be less than fifty per cent of the total cultivated acreage. Really all the government is doing is to guarantee to take delivery of a minimum of from six to seven bushels on the cultivated acreage. Take my own farm, as an example. The specified acreage is forty per cent of the cultivated acreage that is sown to grain. All the government is guaranteeing to me is that they will take delivery of a minimum of five and a half bushels to the acre. I think the minister will agree that that is not a very big guarantee.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I do not. for one minute doubt the sincerity of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I know both those gentlemen would like to see the government committed to taking delivery of all wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950. The Minister of Agriculture is on record, as reported on page 631 of Hansard, in the following words:
Mr. Quelch:	I should like to make it clear
that, as far as this group is concerned, we shall bitterly oppose any proposal to limit the price of $1.35 a bushel to less than the total production during the period in question.
Mr. Gardiner:	You will not oppose it any
more strenuously than I will.
Nobody thinks that this bill as it is worded at the present time commits the government to accept all the wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950. While I do not doubt the sincerity of the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on the other hand I doubt seriously the intentions of the government in this regard. If it was the intention of the government to accept all wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950, why have they not put it in the bill? They have had recommendations from various farm organizations; they have had the statement of their Minister of Agriculture along that line; they have had recommendations from this side and other parts of the house. Why do they bring down a bill which commits the government only to accepting a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre?
If the government really intend to take all the wheat offered for sale they should not hesitate to amend subsection 2 of section 17 to that effect. We may have an election this year, or if we do not have one this year we shall probably have one next year. If we have an election, in all probability the government will be defeated.
That is what you think.
I do not want to prophesy in that regard, but I think the government will admit there is a possibility that they will be defeated.
You are wrong.

I shall leave that to the
opinion of each individual member. There is a possibility that the government will be defeated. If that happens, what do we have? We have merely an act guaranteeing that the government will take a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre on a specified acreage, or about six or seven bushels per acre of the total grain acreage of a farm. It is all very well for members of the Liberal party 83166-48
to say, "Oh, yes, but the Minister of Agriculture said he would oppose any measure that did not provide for the taking of all the wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950". That would not have any effect upon a government that might come in after the next election. The only thing that will govern will be the act and therefore it is essential that, before the committee rises, that section should be amended. I am hoping that the minister will clarify the situation before we go into committee and show definitely what is the intention of the government.
What is the deciding factor in this whole question? I believe at the present time it is the forgotten factor. I refer to the matter of fair dealing with the farmer.
In the early part of this agreement the farmer is making a considerable sacrifice. He is losing anywhere from fifty to seventy five cents a bushel. In compensation for that loss, the government guarantees to take a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre at $1.35 a bushel. The loss is being suffered on all wheat offered for sale, a loss of anywhere from fifty to seventy-five cents on every bushel offered for sale. Then surely the compensatory feature should also guarantee that that $1.35 a bushel would be paid on all wheat offered for sale. How can you balance a loss on total production against compensation on a part of production? It does not make sense or justice. Instead of $1.35 a bushel, we think the price should have been $1.55, which is the price at which we are selling to Britain. But that is not our main contention.
Our main objection is this, that the government is guaranteeing to take only fourteen bushels to the acre, instead of guaranteeing to take the total production offered for sale up to July 31, 1950. The government should guarantee to take all the wheat, or its guarantee becomes to a large extent worthless. If in the next two or three years there is a wheat shortage, if crops are poor, the price of wheat will be maintained at probably a high level and will remain there. Then the guarantee become absolutely useless. If that should be the situation over the next two or three years the farmers of this country, as a result of this agreement, are going to lose several hundred million dollars. But we are hoping that that will not be the situation. We all hope that there will be an ample wheat production, that there will be large crops, in which case the price of wheat will very likely fall within the next two or three years and elevators may easily become congested. That is the reason why the guarantee is needed to take care of a situation where, the elevators

Canadian Wheat Board Act

being congested, the government may have difficulty in taking delivery of the wheat. Unfortunately, however, the bill ignores that situation entirely because it guarantees to take only fourteen bushels to the acre. We feel that the government could very well guarantee, by utilizing farm storage, to take delivery of all the wheat produced. I quite realize that, if the elevators are full, the government cannot take delivery at the elevators, but there is no reason why it could not take delivery through a system of farm storage, to which I shall refer later. But we must recognize the possibility of there being congestion and therefore a possibility of the government being unable to accept delivery at the elevators. I shall leave that question for a moment to speak on the broad principle of an international wheat agreement.
We in this group have for several years, ever since we have been in this house, supported the principle of an international wheat agreement between the great wheat exporting nations of the world. We feel that there should be a long-term agreement in order to encourage high production and in order to stabilize farm prices at a level that will be fair to both producer and consumer. It is well to remember that the new world order which we used to hear so much about during the war but which we do not hear so much about today was to promote security throughout the world. Security throughout the world requires stock-piles of food. I think we all realize today that it is essential that stockpiles of food should be established in as many countries as possible. But unfortunately in the past stock-piles of wheat have invariably been used as an excuse to force down the price of wheat on the open market. Therefore in the future we have to establish a system whereby stock-piles may be maintained without forcing down the price of wheat.
I believe that the wheat agreement with Britain was fully justified but it does entail in its early stages a considerable sacrifice on the part of our farmers. We feel that the sacrifice should be borne by the people of Canada as a whole, and that is why we are so concerned about the guarantee that the government makes regarding the acceptance of fourteen bushels to the acre, which is supposed to remove the sacrifice from the farmers and place the burden squarely on the backs of the Canadian people.
In the future, we believe that wheat agreements should be made between all the wheat producing and wheat consuming nations. I say that we support the agreement with Britain, but at the same time we feel that the

solution of this problem requires international agreements to be made between all wheat producing and wheat consuming nations.
We believe that the proposal for an international wheat quota is absolutely sound in order to ensure orderly marketing, so that in a year of surpluses exporters will have their fair share of the market. It is also needed to encourage maximum production. Otherwise nations might very well restrict their production in order to maintain prices at a high level.
We believe that, in order to carry out our part in providing ample quantities of food in the world, the storage facilities in Canada will have to be greatly expanded and improved. We also believe that importing nations should assume responsibility for building up storage facilities within their own country for stockpiles of food, depending, of course, on the type of food needed.
I am not for one moment an alarmist, but I believe that it would be a very good thing if the European countries established storage warehouses under ground. Scientists tell us that old disused mines may be air-conditioned and used as storage space. I am not suggesting that there will be another war. You do not insure a house against fire because you want a fire. You insure against a loss that might occur through fire. Similarly I think it would be well that large warehouses should be established under ground in Europe as a precaution against war and serious sabotage.
We believe that in Canada the storage facilities should be greatly decentralized and that the government should establish a policy of farm storage, so that bins built to government specifications can be utilized for storage in times of surpluses. A system of government-approved farm storage would simplify the change-over from one pool period to another in the event of congestion. I believe that such a system of farm storage could very well be in operation before July 31, 1950, and the government would then have no difficulty in taking delivery of all the wheat offered. Such a policy of government-approved storage was in operation, I believe, in certain states of the United States during the war. I quite realize that there are difficulties in establishing such a policy, but they are difficulties which, if we seriously address ourselves to them can, I believe, be solved.
In closing^ I wish to say a few words regarding the whole question of price. We in this group stand four-square for a policy of parity prices. That is a price which will give the farmer his fair share of the national income, so that the income of our farming population will bear the same relationship to the national income as our farm population

Canadian Wheat Board Act
bears to the national population. We know very well that that has not been the case in the past and that farmers have not received parity. The only period in which agriculture in this country has received parity was in the years from 1915 to 1919. At that time the farm population was one-third of the national population and farm income was one-third of the national income. From 1926 to 1929 our farm population received one-sixth of the national income; and from 1930 to 1940, one-tenth. I understand that at the present time the farmers receive approximately twenty per cent of the national income, or still around ten per cent below parity.
I have often heard people ask the question, would an international agreement not interfere with a system of parity? I would say, on the contrary, international agreements would greatly help the government in establishing parity within the country, because it would safeguard the government against the danger of slump and make it that much easier for the government to balance their exports and imports. Let us remember that the price to the producer would not necessarily be the same as the price under the international agreement. It would be purely an accident if the price were the same. In all probability the price to the producer would be generally higher than the price obtained under the international agreement.
The question of course is asked: how would a parity price be paid, and who meets the cost of parity price? I would say that the cost of maintaining a parity price would be met automatically through prices; that is to say, if the payment of a parity price resulted in an increased demand in relation to supply the price level would rise, absorbing the increased demand. If, on the other hand, as a result of parity price payments, production increased equally to the increase in demand, there would be no increase in the price level and the parity price payments would be met by increased production. And parity payments would unquestionably greatly stimulate production in this country.
We in this group believe that stabilized agriculture throughout the world would greatly help to stabilize the world economy. I believe history proves conclusively that where you have a prosperous agriculture you have a prosperous nation. We are satisfied that in order to build up the prosperity of the nation, and the prosperity of the grain grower under this agreement, it will be necessary to have an amendment to subsection 2 of section 17 definitely committing the government to the acceptance of all wheat produced and offered 83166-48J
for sale prior to July 31, 1950. I hope the minister will give that assurance when he replies.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. C. MILLER (Portage la Prairie):
speechtext:
Coming from a province that is reckoned as one of the greater wheat growing provinces of the dominion, and from a constituency that is also reckoned as without parallel in the wheat growing industry, I should like to say something on the bill. Government speakers and some of the members of the C.C.F. suggest that we of the Progressive Conservative group are, first of all, against the wheat agreement; second, that we are favouring interests other than the farmers to the prejudice of the farmers; and, third, that this group is against the wheat board. I do not suggest for a moment that hon. members opposite are not acting in good faith, but at the same time I ask for this group on this side of the house the same recognition of our honourable desire to benefit the farmers and to advance their interests.
Hon. members of various political groups may differ as to the methods that are to be followed, but surely we all desire that the best treatment possible should be accorded to the farmers, because the welfare and prosperity of the farmers are so desperately vital to the welfare and the economy of the nation. Any of us who come from the west must unreservedly and immediately acknowledge that our dependence is mainly on agriculture, it does not matter what our occupations may be. It does not necessarily follow that because we are dependent on agriculture we are farmers. Whatever our occupations may be, whether one is a farmer, whether one is a businessman, whether we are professional men or men of labour, the same thing is true, that directly or indirectly all of us who live west of the great lakes depend for our prosperity and our very existence upon the prosperity and welfare of the farmers of the west.
Most of us living in the western country have close friends; some of us have relatives, who depend for their livelihood upon the prosperity of the farming community. If we admit all these things, Mr. Speaker, it is certainly beyond me how any hon. member in any part of the house can suggest for one minute that we on this side would countenance or support any policy or principle that was designed to create, or which would result in creating, hardship or discrimination to or against the western farmer.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) the other day set up and knocked down a few straw men in this house when he
Canadian Wheat Board Act

predicated much of his argument, directed against this group on this side of the house, upon the supposition that we were opposed to the security of the farmer.
We want the farmers to have security, but we feel that the government of this country is not giving them security. For instance, we are often alarmed at the price provided by the British wheat agreement. That agreement has been made and we are prepared to honour it, but I feel that a better price could have been obtained and should have been secured in the negotiations between this country and Great Britain.
I contend, as members on this side have urged time and again, that the government, out of the treasury of the country, should increase the payments to be made to the farmer on all grain that is delivered and sold under the British wheat agreement. That is our position. I also maintain that the farmers have been left in a vulnerable position. Their costs have mounted even since the agreement was signed and will continue to mount, but very little is proposed to be done by the government to give them any security if the cost of production equals or exceeds the selling price to Britain.
That situation is virtually upon us now, that costa of production to the western farmer are virtually exceeding, or at least equalling, the selling price to the British people under the British agreement, and that is the very situation about which we on this side of the house, and particularly this group, have been urging the government long before this session came into being.
The hon. member for Rosthern also said that the farmers are entitled to an assurance of income the same as the people in any industry or occupation. I agree. That is our contention. The hon. member for Rosthern thinks the farmers have security and stability by virtue of the British agreement. I believe the farmers are already getting into a precarious state of insecurity because of the rising costs of production that are setting in every day. I shall be satisfied with the British contract price if the government of this country will give an assurance that they will supplement the price to the farmer on wheat sold by the farmers under the contract price of the British agreement; and the supplement should be made out of the consolidated revenue, out of the treasury, as the hon. member who preceded me said.
The government and the hon. member for Rosthern suggest that farm leaders mostly support this British wheat agreement and the price that was secured under it I think the

example given the other day in the house was an organization known as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Already apparently, the officials of that very organization are deeply concerned with the very problem I have raised tonight, namely, the rising costs of production; and if newspaper articles are to be accepted as a fact, those very officials are shortly-if they have not already been here-coming to Ottawa to discuss that very feature of the farmers' problem.
Let me repeat for the record the statement so often made by hon. members on this side which hon. members of the government and also of the C.C.F. refuse even to hear, namely, that repudiation by Canada of the British wheat agreement is not being and never has been urged by any of us. We say that the farmers have been done an injustice in that the sale price was too low, but we do not and have not urged repudiation. We say that the price should be supplemented, so that the entire nation and not the farmers alone should bear the burden of cheap wheat to Great Britain.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) a few days ago announced in the house the correction of one injustice at least to the farmers. At long last the burden of the loss on wheat for domestic consumption is to be more equitably borne by the nation as a whole and not by the farmers alone. I do not know how much the farmers have already lost by getting thirty cents a bushel below even the British price for wheat for home consumption, but I could hazard a guess, and I think it would be a pretty close one. In any event, the minister admits an injustice and corrects it, but he corrects it only as of a few days ago. The hon. member for Rosthern-and I am using him because he spoke on this point- admits that even he saw this injustice more than a year ago, and took it up with the department at that time. But he is happy now that at long last the Minister of Trade and Commerce has corrected this injustice to the farmers. He is apparently satisfied to forget that that injustice he saw over one year ago has continued since then, and he does not worry about what has happened to the farmers in the interval.
If the minister wants to do complete justice to the western farmer in this respect, he will make amends in full and he will make his thirty cents a bushel increase on wheat for home consumption retroactive, paying the money into the present or the future participation pool which will ultimately be divided among the farmers of this western country. I urge the minister yet to give consideration to

Canadian Wheat Board Act
this angle. If the government does not do this, it seems to me that the farmers of the western provinces are being deprived of at least $30,000,000-and I think it is more-for the period of, say, the preceding eighteen months. I urge the minister to give the farmers their due. There is no reason why the farmers should finance this domestic sale of grain to the tune of $30,000,000 or whatever the amount would be. I fix that $30,000,000 in this way. A newspaper article a few days ago calculated it and estimated that, by the minister making that announcement the other day, he made it possible for the farmers of the west to receive an additional $10,000,000. That would be, roughly, in a period of six months. Therefore in the preceding eighteen months I suggest that a fair estimate is that sum of $30,000,000 which I have mentioned.
I say the country should do this, financing it out of the general revenues. I do not agree on the necessity of making the feeders of grain pay any increased price. I do not say it is wrong, but I cannot see at the moment where it is right that the feeders of this grain should not have some subsidy or something to ensure that they do not pay an increased amount. But I think the farmers should get an increased amount because they should not have to finance millers, or feeders of any kind.
Some hon. members opposite delight in suggesting that we on this side are saying that Britain will not honour her agreement. No one has a greater appreciation of the honour of Great Britain than I have. But while I do not suggest that Great Britain will dishonour her agreement, I do say that the agreement leaves loopholes, not for repudiation or for dishonouring, but for misunderstanding. Let me read from this wheat agreement, or a part of it, as reported in Hansard of August 15, 1946, at page 4848. I am going to read only one small part. It is section 2 (a), which provides the method of fixing the price per bushel of the grain to be delivered under this agreement for the various years. In particular, I wish to read paragraphs (iii) and (iv) of section 2 (a), which are as follows:
(iii)	in respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1948-49, not less than $1.25.
(iv)	in respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1949-50, not less than $1.
Then paragraph (b):
The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year il948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December,
1947,	and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December,
1948.	In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the
United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years, and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
The point is this, Mr. Speaker. They agreed on a floor of $1.25 and $1 respectively, and provided for further negotiations. If wheat on the world market in 1948, 1949 and 1950 is, say, $2 a bushel or even $1.50, then Canada may be bound to deliver for $1.25 or for $1, as the case may be, according to tihe year, if Great Britain says so; because it is stipulated in that contract, if you read it one way, that they shall deliver so many million bushels in those years. Canada and Great Britain will negotiate. The agreement says so. But they may not come to an agreement that Britain is to pay more than 'the floor. If that happens, Canada would be annoyed for Canada might be justified in saying, "If you do not give us more than the floor of $1.25 or $1, as the case may be, we will negotiate but not agree." Then what would happen? Would the deal be off? Suppose they did negotiate according to the terms of this agreement, but did not agree. What would be the position? Would Canada have to deliver at $1.25 or $1, or would the deal be off because on further negotiations Canada and Great Britain could not agree? Or in their negotiations Great Britain might say, "Yes, we are going to take into consideration the fact that you gave us cheap wheat in 1946, but we think $1.35 is about right." Canada might and, if the price of wheat was up pretty high, likely would want more. Would this agreement fall, then; or, if not, wha't umpire is to tell us what the price of wheat should be in those years? The agreement says there is to be a sort of floor, and they are going to negotiate the question and tell us; but that agreement is absolutely silent, and no one can tell us who is to say what the price will be if, following negotiations, the two contracting parties cannot agree on any price at all over and above the floor.
My suggestion, then, is that within the four corners of this agreement there is room, not for dishonour, not for repudiation, but for squabbling, misunderstanding, disagreement and bad feeling between Great Britain and Canada, which should not be the case. Might not this agreement even terminate at the end of the first two years if the two governments could not agree, each thinking the other to be unreasonable? Each might be justified in thinking the other unreasonable. Let me suggest to either the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that he ask twenty-five lawyers in succession what the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

clauses I have just read mean., and I venture to suggest that there would be twenty-five very peculiar answers.
Whether what I have said is right or whether some other hon. member has offered the right suggestion; whatever may be the situation, I deplore the suggestion of some hon. members on the government side and some hon. members speaking for the C. C. F. party that they alone have the interests of the western producers at heart. I am deeply concerned about the economic welfare of the farmers of western Canada, and I will not take a back seat to any hon. member on that score.
There is some suggestion from some hon. members of other parties that our group are opposed to the Canadian wheat board.
Hear, hear.

I know of no one on this side who is opposed to a wheat board; certainly I am not. My attitude throughout on that point has been clear and consistent.
In regard to the deferring of payments on participation certificates, however, I wish to say this. I am in favour of those holding certificates participating in the profits for that year. I am opposed to having the farmers' money kept for distribution until 1950. If they were to get it by 1950 it might not be so bad, but I hazard the guess that it will be closer to 1955 than 1950 before they get any money, if they ever do get any. Take this example. Suppose farmer A had a big summer-fallow in 1945. He was put to a great deal of expense in getting that summer-fallow in shape. In our part of the country at least, they usually sow wheat on summer-fallow. In 1946 he sowed it to wheat and, as it turned out, he was fortunate because we had a very large crop last year. This wheat, remember, is now being sold; it is moving to the market, and is bringing what even the government expect will be the highest price we shall receive for wheat in the period from 1945 to 1950. All right. This farmer may not sow wheat on that summer-fallow again before 1950. He may get one more crop of wheat, but it is possible and very likely, the way they farm nowadays, that he will not sow another crop of wheat, certainly not on that particular land; he may have another little strip somewhere else, but I doubt if between 1946 and 1950 he will have another wheat crop on this land he summer-fallowed in 1945.
This farmer should be entitled to participate in the profits on his 1946 wheat, and payments to him on his participation certificates should be and normally would be very material. But is he allowed to get those profits? No.

According to the decision of this government, he is being made to donate those profits to a participation pool for the purpose of supporting an alleged stabilization scheme proposed by the government. And remember, Mr. Speaker, that stabilization is to be carried on in the years at the end of the contract, 1948-49 and 1949-50, when this government visualize much lower wheat prices. I suggest that the government are taking credit for a grand, original stabilization scheme. They are letting the farmers of the west believe that the government is creating this stabilization fund, that government money is being used to make the payments of $1.35 a bushel every year. It is not the government's money. It is the money of farmer A, whom I mentioned a few moments ago, and of thousands of other farmers, which is being retained by this government to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars and will be retained until 1950, to stabilize this so-called government scheme. It is not the government that is doing the stabilizing at all; it is John Jones and the other farmers who are stabilizing that scheme.
I believe in stabilization. The government say they are doing it; I say they are not. They are making the farmers of Canada donate their profits in order that this price may be stabilized. I believe the farmers should get all their profits each year, with a guarantee from this or any other government in office in Canada that the price will be maintained at a decent floor level, and that from the treasury of this country the government-not the farmers-will donate the money necessary to maintain this stabilization fund and provide at least a fair floor price during the years of low wheat prices which the government envisage.
I do not like these regulations. I have always opposed them, particularly under the old wheat board act. There is too much power in the bureaucrats; there is too much regimentation. In this case a great many regulations to which I as a practising solicitor have objected in past years have been embodied in the proposed statute, so that much of my objection has been overcome. However, we, the people of Canada, are putting the wheat board into big business, and I do not believe we should place them in too much of a strait jacket by including everything in this proposed statute. After all, we cannot foresee the eventualities that may arise in handling these millions of bushels of grain, and I admit that some latitude must be given the board to make orders and regulations so that they may efficiently and properly carry on their business. But let me suggest to the minister that, in the past, many of the prose-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
cutions under these regulations were completely uncalled for. Perhaps my view has been coloured by the fact that I happened to be defence counsel in a great many of these trials, but I believe that many of the prosecutions were actually unjustified. Certainly over a period of years I convinced myself many times, and convinced the court of appeal of Manitoba once, that the prosecutions undertaken by the wheat board were completely unjustified and uncalled for. If you have a prosecution and you beat the wheat board, as I have been fortunate enough to do on two or three occasions, then they just make new regulations. The next time I went to court my case was out of court because they had fixed it in the meantime. They were the champion Mr. Fixit. In the new bill proposed, this should be taken into consideration, too.
It would be fairer if the expenses of the board were paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. I am afraid some may think I am giving that fund quite a ride.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Nevertheless I am serious in that, and I think it is of great importance. I do not believe that the cost of operating this expensive set-up should be taken out of the proceeds of the sale of farmers' crops. It is too expensive a set-up for farmers to handle.
This expensive way of handling our western crop is devised not only for the welfare of the farmers but because it is essential to the welfare and economic stability of the country as a whole. That is why I say that the expense of this seemingly almost top-heavy organization should be paid from the common funds of the country, and should not be deducted from the moneys the farmers should receive from the sale of their grain. The expenses should be paid by the whole nation.
I am afraid that the cost of operation of the board with its hundreds, yes, its thousands, of officials, none of whom is underpaid, will take a large slice from the farmers' receipts. If the country would undertake that expense and relieve the participation pools to that extent-and I believe I am right when I say the participation pools bear it-then there would be larger participation payments for the farmers.
One further point, and I shall have finished. The penalties which have always appeared in the regulations, and which are carried forward by this measure, are too high. Imagine the spectacle of a solicitor employed by the board standing in the court room of a small town in a western province, as I have seen them, and asking the magistrate sitting on the bench to impose on a farmer, or on some poor unsuspecting elevator agent who has accepted delivery of sixty bushels of wheat too much, a fine of $500 or $1,000! Imagine that solicitor coming out from the city of Winnipeg, and being paid by the wheat board-
That is the real grievance.

I will say this to the hon. member for Winnipeg South that the board did me the honour of asking me to act for the board. On the occasion I have in mind, the solicitor asked that the magistrate impose the outrageous penalty of something like $500 or $1,000. Why, the man I was defending turned forty different colours.
I have told this story because I wish to make clear the pure silliness of asking a penalty of $5,000. We might as well make it a reasonable one. If we did so, there would be more uniformity in the penalities imposed throughout the western provinces, instead of having one man fined $10 for an offence and, a few towns farther down the line, another man being fined $50 or $100 for the same offence. If the penalities were brought down they would be more in keeping with the offences committed, if any are committed, under the act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to congratulate the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I was almost going to do the same for the last speaker, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller). He made a most commendable speech, and presented it well. Indeed, I believe if the Liberals had chosen him he would have been on this side of the house, right now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You ought to know.

However, his task, sitting where he now sits, will be a most difficult one, if he ever hopes to obtain any results for the farmers. There are on that side of the house three sincere Conservatives who are representing the farmers. I am not going to give their names at the present time, but I know them all very well, and all happen to come from Manitoba. So that if those three Manitoba members ever hope, from where they now sit, to get anything for the farmers, it will be a sorry day for them.
This wheat agreement is a long-term agreement, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) should be congratulated upon it. It would have been disastrous if the government had asked the people of Great Britain, who were in such dire circumstances at the time, to buy wheat at a price they could not afford. Further-
Canadian Wheat Board Act

more, I believe it was the intention of the government to encourage other nations not to grow wheat, and to make long-term wheat agreements with other countries, so that different nations could trade with us, and we could take their commodities in return.
It is all very fine for some hon. members opposite, under the cloak of the Progressive Conservative party, to put up a big fight for the farmers; but had the hon. member who has just taken his seat sat in the house in 1932, I suggest that he would have found it most awkward if he had attempted to defend the position in which farmers were placed at that time when they-and I had the same experience-sold No. 1 wheat at the elevator for thirty-one cents a bushel. I have nothin* further to say at this time, except that I shall support this measure to the fullest extent.

Is the house ready for
the question?

Mr. Speaker,
I think we have to hear from a couple of ministers at least. Meantime, however, while they are getting material together, I shall have a few observations to make.
First of all, may I say we propose to respect and honour agreements entered into with other nations. I believe that is taken for granted. May I also add that I support in every particular the necessity for the continuance of the Canadian wheat board. I hope that is clear to hon. members to my left.
What about the grain exchange?

I shall deal with
that before I take my seat, and make it very clear, too. If it is necessary to supply the people in Great Britain with cheap wheat, then the contribution should be made by the entire population of Canada; not by one section, the farmers, as it is being done today. I think we are all fairly clear on that point.
The avowed principle of the bill is to make provision for meeting the requirements of the contract with the United Kingdom. The price provided in the agreement is the vital part of the bill. I should like to put a question or two with respect to the great obscurity of this measure on that point. The relevance of this question is obvious because of its direct relation to the initial price of *1.35 which the Canadian wheat board is authorized to pay to farmers. This may be too high or too low, depending upon the [Mr. Sinnott.l
answers given to the questions which I wish to propound. Clause 2 (b) of the agreement reads:
The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any diiference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
I wish to emphasize the last few lines. I hope the people get that clearly. No one with whom I am associated impugns the good faith of the United Kingdom government. Let us be clear on that. That is not the issue, that Great Britain will keep her word. But we have some doubts about this contract and we should like to have them cleared up. We should like to know what the wording of that contract actually means. I know it is idle to speculate as to what interpretation the United Kingdom now puts or may later put upon the words in that agreement; but there is one thing we can and should do now, that is, put upon the record in public and imperishable form, for every Canadian farmer to see and hear, what interpretation Canada puts upon these words in that agreement. What did we mean by these words when we signed:
The United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
That is the point I should like to have cleared up and I think there is one minister in particular who may be able to do that. In his speech in Montreal in December last before the Montreal local of the agricultural institute of Canada, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said:
The third provision is the important one from the point of view of those who are impressed by the arguments of the grain exchange. In their advertisements they ask this definite question:	"What guarantee have you that because
vou accept a lower price now, you will get a higher price later?"
My answer is this provision in the contract: in determining the price for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50 the United Kingdom overnment will have regard to any difference etween the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and the 1947-48 crop years.
The grain exchange say in their advertising there is no guarantee at all and don't let anyone tell you anything to the contrary. It isn't true.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
All I can say in reply is that I personally discussed the matter with the British officials and their minister. They have agreed that we are entitled to have possible losses in the first two years made up in the last two. They have so stated in the contract.
In the same speech the hon. gentleman also said:
In so far as agreements made by Britain with other nations are concerned they are only for short terms, most of them from year to year. Those will be the best evidence to show what Canadian farmers are entitled to in the last two years to make up for any losses they may have taken in the first two years.
Those seem to be plain words, but we want to be sure that the way they are being interpreted by the Canadian farmer is not contrary to the meaning intended by the right hon. gentleman. Despite the fact that it is the Department of Trade and Commerce which handled this agreement, I think we all understand that it was the Minister of Agriculture who really negotiated this deal and who, with all due respect to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), probably knows more about the deal than any other member of the government at this time.
I remember reading the statement by one of his advisers, Mr. Hannam, head of the federation of agriculture. Last fall he told the farmers that they had one choice, either to accept this wheat deal between the United Kingdom and Canada or to market their grain on the open market through the Winnipeg grain exchange. I consider that statement was extreme and misleading to the wheat producers of Canada, because I do not think they had only that choice as he put it. I will deal with that a little later.
I think we could have had a different agreement negotiated without having to deliver our wheat on the open market or to the Winnipeg grain exchange. I do not think the president of the federation of agriculture was as tolerant as he might have been. Quite often, people are carried away in their antagonism to the grain exchange. As is well known, I have no brief for the Winnipeg grain exchange.
On February 22, just last Saturday, the price of No. 2 Canadian export wheat was quoted at $2.51 a bushel. Durum wheat was quoted at ten cents above that, or $2.61. The last time we were discussing this bill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the wheat board had sold export wheat at that time for $2.49, whereas the United Kingdom agreement price is $1.55. Does the Minister of Agriculture agree that on sales completed today we enter in the actual, not possible, loss column an item of ninety-four cents a bushel?
That is something that might be cleared up when he speaks on this matter with a simple answer "yes" or "no".
A few days ago the United Kingdom made a short-term agreement with the Argentine at a price, according to published newspaper accounts, of $3.21 a bushel. If that is the best evidence to show what Canadian farmers are entitled to in the last two years, ninety-four cents a bushel will be much too low a loss to enter in the accounts. These two current illustrations must show how hopelessly vague the matter has been left, even with the explanations given in Montreal last December by the Minister of Agriculture.
Before voting upon this bill which so vitally affects the well-being of a large number of Canadians, this house in fairness is entitled to know, beyond all chance of misunderstanding, what interpretation this government now puts upon the clause in the agreement which I have read, and what interpretation it will urge should be put upon it by the United Kingdom government. I can put the issue very simply and directly.
If not later than December of this year, when the actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-40 are being negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom and Canada, the world price of wheat is the same as it is today and the average world price of wheat throughout the 1946-47 crop year has been $2.49 a bushel, will Canada urge upon the United Kingdom government that as there has been a difference of ninety-four cents between the price paid under the agreement and the world price for wheat; as regard must be had for this difference, and as, according to the Minister of Agriculture, we are entitled to have this loss made up, the contract price for 1948-49 should then be $3.43 a bushel.
My example of price is as good as any other for the purpose of finding out what we say or think the agreement actually means in detail. The hon. minister can take any figure or price he likes for the purpose of putting our position upon the record. Let him, if he will, assume that, when setting the 194950 price, the world price is $1, but the average world price throughout the contract has been such that a loss has been sustained by Canada of seventy-five cents a bushel. Now will Canada contend that the contract price for 1949-50 must be $1.75 a bushel? That question should be plainly answered.
These are not academic or hypothetical questions, but of the greatest relevance and importance in coming to a conclusion on the vital price terms of this bill. It may be that our interpretation of the contract is such that
Canadian Wheat Board Act

if we had it clarified and confirmed by the United Kingdom government, we could be much more generous-I prefer the term "more fair"-to the Canadian farmer in fixing the initial price of SI .35.
You read a good section of it and it was quite clear.

I think the minister
should explain exactly how he interprets it. I have also a question to put to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A lot of questions were asked on the orders of the day this afternoon about the price of feed grain, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce should clear up a vital point and tell us how much the feeder in Canada is required to pay for feed wheat today and how much he has been required to pay since 1942. The minister should also tell us how much the producer of that wheat receives per bushel, as well as the number of bushels of wheat consumed annually for feed in Canada since 1942. There has been considerable misunderstanding on this point and I think the minister should put the figures on Hansard, because a great many people are interested in knowing just what the facts are.
I wish to endorse what was said by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), with respect to establishing farm storage facilities in Canada. It will be remembered that in the early years of the war provision was made by the government for the storage of wheat on Canadian farms when the elevators were full. I trust that provision will be made for adequate farm storage.	,
I also hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture will tell us more definitely than they did the other day whether any limitation will be placed on the acreage production of wheat during the term of the five-year contract with the British government. The bill as I read it is a little vague on that point.
I am much concerned as to my attitude on this bill in the absence of a definite statement from the responsible minister as to whether a limit will be placed on the wheat acreage or wheat deliveries for sale at any time in the life of the agreement. I think the house and the country are entitled to an unequivocal statement from the minister on that point.
I said that I would state where I stand on the Winnipeg grain exchange. I do not know why the C.C.F. should keep asking me what my attitude is with regards to the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. I doubt if any other mem-
Because we represent the farmers.

I doubt if any other ber of this house has done more than I have in my humble but sincere way ever since I came into this house to promote the welfare of the western farmer. If anybody cares to look up the record they will find that on March 30, 1943, as reported at page 1698 of Hansard of that session, the then member for Qu'Appelle and myself moved the following resolution:
The policy of the government with respect to the marketing of Canadian field crops is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken forthwith to provide for the marketing of coarse grains as well as of wheat, by the Canadian wheat board, within the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 and amendments thereto; and that action should be taken immediately to abolish trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange in order to prevent speculation and profiteering at the expense of the farmers.
Surely that is clear enough for anybody!
Do you still stand by that?

I am still standing right on my own feet, and you usually know where I stand. At the time that resolution was put to a vote on March 30, 1943, the government voted solidly against it. Yet that same government, in that same year, on September 28, 1943, passed an order in council doing exactly what we had asked them to do in that resolution. Surely that is clear enough for anybody.
That was after two byelections.

I do not know anything about that. What I do say is that I have been consistent right along in my attitude toward the Winnipeg grain exchange, and as long as the wheat board1 continues to operate I do not care whether the grain exchange operates or not if it can find any business for itself. We are living in a democracy and should be tolerant of all. I am out to get the best deal I can for the western producer, who has not had any too good a deal in the past.
I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will rise in his place and give us detailed information on the points I have raised and that, following him, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will answer the questions I have put to him. Then we shall have a clear understanding of what we should do with respect to this legislation, which has an important bearing on the marketing of our future wheat crops.

Mr. Speaker, I join in this debate with some reluctance, as a sheer matter of compulsion. The studied silence of the two ministers who are dealing with this matter compels me to rise in my place and say at least a couple of things.
Of course I am a farmer, as all hon. members know, farming the public from a law office. But I have lived in that section of the country for a long, long time and I want to say a word about the Winnipeg grain exchange. I have listened to this twitting which has come from my left for some considerable time. I have this to say about the Winnipeg grain exchange or anyone else. I am ready to condemn them or anyone else when it is proven that they do not function in the interests of the country. Until that is done, I do not intend to join in the hysteria which exists to my immediate left and try to get popular with people by complaining of individuals simply because they have made a little money. I heard the other day about a man who died worth $250,000. I do not know who he was, but I wish he had left half a million, if he had brains enough to make it. I should like to see him do even better.
I can see no reason why the Winnipeg grain exchange should not operate at this moment. I cannot see that it has anything to do with the operation of the wheat board. If the operation of a wheat board is the best way to dispose of our grain, let us do it in that way. But you are going to operate it now by compulsion, and compulsion suits my hon. friends to the left, because they know that neither their philosophy nor the philosophy of any other ism can exist without compulsion and dictatorship from the top.
Why should a farmer not be able to sell his grain to me if I can do a better job for him than the wheat board? I am not criticizing the wheat board. The chief officer of the board who was sitting here has been a friend of mine for thirty-five years. At one time when he was a poor man he was a client of mine. Perhaps that is why he rose to his present position. His predecessor, Mr. Murray, was also a very good friend of mine. I am not for a moment suggesting that these men are not doing the best they can, that they are not doing a good job. But what that has to do with giving the farmer an option of disposing of his produce through one channel more than another is utterly beyond me. I may believe in the wheat board; I may believe they are doing a good job and hope they will continue to do so. But if I, a farmer, granted I were a farmer, sitting on that prairie thought
I could do better by using some method of marketing, I would not want my neighbours to come and say, "You do it this way and this way only". In that direction lies socialism, in that direction lies dictatorship, and it can operate in no other way.
That is my view of the Winnipeg grain exchange and the wheat board. Remember that the only time the Winnipeg grain exchange has ever been abolished in the dominion, and trading on it abolished., was on a rising market. Trading was never abolished on a falling market. Having said that, I am not in a position, nor is anyone else I know of here in a position to form a judgment, whether good or bad; and so we have asked and I ask again that we have a committee of this house to which we can let these people come and tell their story.
I have not a client on that grain exchange; not a single grain company have I now, nor have I had for twenty years. But I will not condemn somebody; my instincts and training both forbid me to condemn anyone, without a hearing, either the grain exchange or the wheat board or a grain dealer or anyone else. Perhaps trading should be abolished. They are having a lot of fun with a little bit of rye they have there now-and I mean the rye grown on the ground. I watch the papers, and it is doing some quick dances. But I have not yet heard anyone in this house give me one reason, to show where the farmer lost any money dealing on the open market while there was an open market.
I cannot help thinking of the United States; I cannot help thinking of Liverpool; I cannot help thinking of the United States first, with infinitely more wheat than we have. The Chicago exchange operates and there is no suggestion anywhere of closing it. It may be that it should be closed. The position is this at the moment : I am unconvinced, and I have listened, to all the reasons -that we have heard in this house. But I Should like to listen to the reasons of the persons who really know.
I know Mr. Justice Turgeon very well. I worked for him when he was attorney general, when Saskatchewan was first formed. He was deputy and then attorney general and I know he is a reasonable man. His commission went through this country as did others and found as a fact that the grain exchange did do a service in the marketing of grain. He may have been wrong. Probably he was. Probably times have changed. But I refuse at the moment to accept the hysteria of a lot of people clamouring against the considered judgment of Mr. Justice Turgeon; and so I again say, let us have a committee and let us
Canadian Wheat Board Act

get at the facts. If these people are no good, let us close them up. If the wheat board are not doing the job we might improve them. That is the position in which I stand with respect to that institution.
Just another word. We have all been asserting our great friendship for Great Britain and I think we as a House of Commons might accept that in its entirety and as applying to every one of us. I do not think we gain much by saying, impliedly at least, that we are the great friends of Britain, that we know she will not dishonour her word, and all these statements made in the air, which really mean nothing.
What is the real situation? I think it is this. I think, if you have a terrible drop in the world price of wheat, no contract anywhere can stop an avalanche of that kind. I think the most we can do is, within ourselves, to support some sort of floor; and if we have a real slide the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows at least how difficult even that is going to be.
I trust I shall not be accused of disloyalty when I say this. In my humble opinion, if in the last two years of this contract, which God forbid, wheat should hit the toboggan, not being disloyal.to England I would say that this House of Commons and the people of this country will not hold up at the point of a gun poor struggling Britons to pay a price away in advance of the world price. I think we are more decent than that.
You are holding them up now.

I will hold you up in a minute and you will be sorry you spoke. I do not want to hold them up and I have never suggested any such thing. We have suggested that the dominion treasury, and not the farmers, should bear the gift to Britain, and I defy the hon. member to say that anything else was ever said by anyone on this side of the house. You have your chance now to reply. Not a word. I knew you would not. So I come back squarely to where I was a moment ago-
That is nowhere.

I really wish I could keep track of these hon. members because, while I have a sense of humour, when I cannot hear them I cannot answer them.
I am sorry about that, but I did not hear the last remark. I come back to this position. In so far as those latter two years are concerned, I do not think they are serious. I do not think the people of this country, granted we have a fall, would ever permit the 
British people to suffer, in the event of foodstuffs rising; and certainly not within the four years has anyone whose remarks I have read foreseen a supply enough to feed the world, to say nothing of a surplus. Those last two years amount to very little. With that, sir, I conclude.

Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce answer the question asked by the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) before we pass the second reading? The question was in connection with the acceptance of all wheat offered for sale prior to the end of July, 1950.
