speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must express some surprise that on an important measure like this the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) did not see fit to make a statement when he was moving second reading of this bill. I had fully expected that he would do so, and I had equally fully expected to follow him and make a statement with respect to the attitude which this party would take on the measure. He did not rise in his place; the Speaker saw someone else and the debate went on. Mr. Speaker now advises us that, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaks, he closes the debate. Under the circumstances,
I think I should take a few minutes to make some observations with respect to this measure

Canadian Wheat Board Act
and to outline clearly where the party I have the honour to lead stands on this bill.
Before I proceed, I should like to make one observation, and by so doing I do not mean to detract from the addresses made by any of the hon. members who have so far spoken. But I do wish to say how much the statement made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) agreed-and I am now speaking generally-with the attitude taken by myself and this party with respect to this great problem of agriculture, and more particularly toward the question of the marketing of wheat. I desire to compliment the hon. member on the clarity of his statement and on the soundness of his views, speaking generally.
Bill No. 23 is a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The Canadian Wheat Board Act is an act that was passed in 1935, twelve years ago. The purpose of that act was to give the wheat farmer some greater stability of income. Under that act, the government undertook to guarantee an initial price; and after the crop was sold and the difference between what was received and what was paid was made up, the government undertook to pay to the farmers the balances left over at the end of each crop year. There was in the bill at that time no power to limit acreage and no power to limit the bushelage per acre, which would be accepted. As I have said, the moneys left, after one year's operations were over, were to be distributed to the farmers on the basis of the crop sold by each farmer.
The history of the initial price paid under this measure since it was passed can be stated briefly. In 1935 it was 87i cents a bushel. In 1939 it was reduced to seventy cents a bushel. In 1942 it was made ninety cents a bushel. During the war under the war measures legislation, by order in council in 1943 the initial price was fixed at $1.25. Then last year it was made $1.35. By order in council during the war years two other things were done. By one order in council the government killed the practice of paying participation certificates at the end of each crop year; and some of those participation certificates were not paid for a period of three, four or more years. Those for the year 1944 are not yet paid and I understand that some of them for 1943 are not paid, although I am not positive as to that. Then, by another order in council this board was given the power to carry out the British agreement. That brings us up to date with respect to the major changes under that act.
I now come to the bill before us. The main purposes of the present bill are outlined opposite one of the initial pages of the
bill itself. If I may be permitted to do so,
I should like to summarize the purposes of the bill as briefly as I can. First, it gives to the government statutory power, through the wheat board, to carry out this British wheat agreement. That is the feature of it which has to do with external or international policy. Second, the bill provides for paying the farmer $1.35 a bushel as an initial price during the period of the British wheat agreement, which is five years altogether, and which ends three or four years from now, in 1950, to be exact. The third purpose of the bill is to enable the government to hold any balance of the farmers' money for five years rather than distribute it at the end of each crop year as was the purpose of the act and the actual policy carried out under the act in its early years. The fourth purpose of the bill is to give the government, through the board, power to take over and sell the farmers' oats, barley, rye and flax in the same manner if it chooses as it now does with wheat, and to do that without any stipulation whatever as to the price to be paid for those crops. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is a fair statement of the main intent and purpose of the bill.
Our attitude toward this bill may be stated briefly. Some of our members, speaking as they have a right to do as individuals, have already stated something of where we stand. I am very glad to have the opportunity now to make it clear for the party generally. We recognize this bill for what it is, a measure made necessary by the government's wheat contract with Britain. We recognize that contract to be an international agreement, an agreement entered into by two nations and officially signed by the recognized representatives of those two nations. As leader of the Progressive Conservative party, I do not propose to dishonour an international agreement. We shall take no step that will result in wrecking that agreement, certainly not without the full concurrence of the other agreeing parties.
Having said that, let me say this also. Let me make clear that we take no responsibility for that contract. It was not brought before us before it was agreed to; and when it was brought before us, after it had been agreed to, we took exception to certain features of the agreement. We did not agree with it then; we do not agree with certain features of it now. We thought the contract was unwise in certain particulars. We thought it was unnecessary, and we thought it was harmful to Canada's international trade. Nevertheless it is a contract entered into between governments and cannot be broken by either side, without the agreement of the other, without dishonour. We recognize it as that, and we
Canadian Wheat Board Act

have no thought whatever of repudiating such an international agreement. All we can do now, all any party can do now; all this parliament can do now is to try to make the best of it, try to see that we make no mistakes in administering it, try as far as we can to correct its ill effects and, if I may be permitted to say so, try to substitute for it, if we can with the approval of the other contracting party, an international wheat agreement which will bring something of stability to international wheat prices. Briefly that is our position with respect to this bill and the agreement.
Having referred to the purposes of the bill, I may be asked: what are the main features of it? In an early page of the bill the purport of it is stated as the government sees it. What, in simple language, are the main features of the bill? It has many features. I shall deal briefly with only four of the main ones. First, the government is taking the right to usurp the powers of the board. If it were in order to refer to the clauses of the bill I would do so, but I am a little afraid I might be asked to sit down if I went on to deal with its clauses. The government is taking the right to usurp the powers of the board. And it is taking the right to extend the powers of the board. And it is taking the right to order the board around in certain important particulars. When we get into committee we shall point out where these things are provided.
Second, and to be more specific, the government is taking the power to possess the farmers' oats, barley, rye and flax in exactly the same way as it has taken power to possess their wheat and control its marketing. It is taking power to sell these crops at any price, even below the world price if it wishes to do so. I say it is taking that power and, that being so it must expect to use it; otherwise why have it in the bill? It is taking blanket power to do with these crops as it does with wheat, but in this case by order in council with no guarantee as to price, no guarantee as to the principle or formula that will be followed in arriving at the prices of these products. That, Mr. Speaker, is wartime order in council legislation in its most high-handed form, carried out now in time of peace.
That is something of the power being left with the board. I say it not by way of criticism at the moment but only by way of analysis of what is contained in this bill. I do not oppose the board taking over coarse grains, but I point out that under this measure it has power to take them over without any guarantee whatever as to the prices it will pay for these commodities.
A third main feature of the bill is that the government is planning to hold large sums of

the farmers' money for a period of five years. Part of that money may be used to offset future losses, but in any event the government is not going to pay participation certificates at the end of each crop year but is planning to hold the money for five years. In other words, money properly owing to the farmers at the end of each crop year is being held by this government under this wheat board for five years, earning rates of interest much lower than the farmers are paying on the money they have to borrow.
A fourth feature of the bill is that the government is taking power to limit the acreage of grain on which it will accept delivery, and it is taking power to limit to as little as fourteen bushels the amount it may accept from each acre. I say those powers are in the bill. As far as those features are concerned, what I want from the government is a statement indicating exactly what it means. Either there is to be a limitation some time on the acreage, if it is necessary, and a limitation on the amount that will be accepted for delivery from each acre, or there is not. As I read the bill, it contains that power. Any man of sense knows the government will never use that power unless it is considered necessary. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) wanted an assurance from the government that it would never be used. What I want from the government is a clear statement. What I expect they will say-I was going to add "if they are perfectly frank" but I will not say that-is that they hope it will never be necessary to use this power; but that having the power, if there should be much more wheat than can be sold, they would use these limiting powers on the delivery of wheat they would accept. I can read nothing different in the bill.
With respect to the wheat agreement I should like to make a few brief observations. The government is giving statutory form to a wheat agreement with Britain. So far this has been done by international agreement; now, under this bill, the administration of the agreement is to be put in statutory form. Second, in this agreement the government has taken blanket authority for five years to market the farmers' wheat. Those things are self-evident. Third, as a result of this agreement, together with the announced domestic policy with respect to the sale of wheat, first at $1.25 a bushel, now at $1.55, for consumption at home, the government is selling the farmers' 1946 wheat crop for $100,000,000 less than that crop would bring at the world market price. That is the estimate. It will probably be more than that.
I tried to get the minister to give an estimate.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I do not blame him for not giving one, but it is very easy to make a calculation. My estimate is on the conservative side.
Then, fourth, as a result of this agreement the government has sold more of the crop to one country than that country has ever used for its own purposes, in a year of peace-many millions more.
No, more than it has received from Canada, not more than it has ever used.

I meant to say that-more than it ever received from Canada. Under this arrangement 160,000,000 bushels is being sold to one country by Canada. The normal amount taken by that country from Canada in the past has been 90.000,000 to 100,000,000 bushels, or thereabouts.
What is the result? Canada cannot depend upon Great Britain alone for a market, important as that market may be. Now, in these critical times, other nations are denied a reasonable share of our grain. What is to be their attitude with respect to trade with us when this arrangement is over, after they have entered into arrangements with other countries for grain, and after those countries have had to pay higher prices than Great Britain is having to pay?
I say the government has sold more of one crop to one country than that country has ever obtained from Canada for its own use in a peacetime year. And the government has sold that portion of the crop at a considerably lesser price than it has sold to other nations. As the minister said the other day, the figure was $1.55 a bushel, and he told me of some sales to other countries which had run up to $2.49. In those two -ways the government has prejudiced our future trade in every land that buys grains.
One other observation with respect to that agreement. The government has excused itself for this kind of bargain by saying that it stabilizes prices to Canadian farmers. In my judgment that is just pure bluff, and nothing else. There can be no stabilized price to the Canadian farmer by an international agreement with one nation, when in that agreement in one year, it pays $1.55; in another year it may pay $1.25 and in another year it may pay $1. It is no stabilization of prices to the Canadian farmer to have an agreement of that kind.
And, Mr. Speaker, there is less stabilization of prices in an agreement of that kind when, at the end of five years, the world price of wheat may be $1 a bushel, even less. If then this nation comes to deal with Great Britain in an
effort to make a new agreement, at what figure will it be made? Perhaps it will be at $1. Perhaps it will be less. Where is the stability to Canadian agriculture arising from an international arrangement of that kind? Any stability that is in this bill, anything that gives stability of price to Canadian farmers, is not in the international agreement at all, but in the domestic arrangement where, after the government sells grain at a large price now, risking a lower price in the future, it proceeds to give to the farmer during the period of this agreement $1.35 a bushel1. That is all the stability there is to farmers' prices; and that does not come from the international agreement. It comes from the domestic arrangement here at home. It could have been done without the international agreement at all. It could have been done even better and at a higher price without that international agreement at all.
As to the government's domestic wheat policy, I shall content myself by making five brief observations. First, the price the government is paying farmers for wheat is less than it is getting for the wheat. The government is getting $1.55 from Great Britain. They are getting $2.40 or $2.50 from some other countries. Just now they are getting $1.55 for wheat sold for local use, although up until now they have been selling the farmers' wheat for Canadian use at $1.25 to make cheap bread for Canadian homes.
I say the price the government is paying farmers is less than the government is getting for the wheat. I say it is less than a fair price. I say it is less than a parity price. If the term "parity" may be taken to mean a fair price, then parity for wheat today is not $1.35, but is $1.55. And under this arrangement the only amount the farmers are assured of getting for these five years is $1.35. There may be something at the end of five years, or there may not; it depends altogether on what happens to the world price in the next three or four years.
In addition to all that, the price the government is paying farmers is less than enough to keep agriculture in an equitable position in the Canadian economy. Anything less than parity will not keep agriculture in a relatively equal position in that economy. I say $1.35 is less than parity, less than a fair price and less than it should be, having regard to the increasing costs of farmers' production.
And the price the government is paying these farmers is not enough to keep the Canadian economy on its present high level of income and employment. As soon as you
Canadian Wheat Board Act

let one section of our economy drop down in purchasing power, immediately, or shortly after, that drop is translated to every; other section. If we let agriculture drop down from the fair position it has held in the last two or three years we are immediately weakening the whole Canadian economy, at the very time when our efforts should be to try to keep a high level of national income and a high level of employment.
Second, with regard to our domestic wheat policy, certain impressions have been left to the effect that the government does not intend to limit sales of wheat by farmers. I say that that impression has been left. Let us have it made clear what the intention is, and what the powers are. But whatever the intention is, the government is, in fact, taking power to limit the amount of wheat it will allow farmers to sell. That is in the bill; I cannot read it in any other way.
Third, the government is asking power to take the farmers' oats, barley, rye and flax, without any guarantee as to price, and without any formula as to how it is to arrive at what is a fair price. The government may say that it does not intend to use that power, but why is it in the bill if it does not intend to use it? I suggest that under the government's policies of undertaking to sell overseas such large quantities of other farm products, bacon, cheese, et cetera, it has tied its own hands. I say that in order to carry out its own undertakings it will be forced to bring in policies to take over the marketing of oats, barley, flax and peas and to sell these crops in this country at less than the world market prices That is one of the consequences of its policies. I am not saying at the moment whether that is a good policy or a bad policy, but I am saying that, in undertaking to supply not only local Canadian needs but so much of the needs of the outside world, the government has tied, its hands with respect to the continuance of such controls as these on the price to be paid for those coarse grains, and oni the interferences to the export of them.
Fourth, the government by adopting such price policies as this is freezing the wheat income of Canada at a level below parity.
I have said that before in substantially similar words. Since wheat prices in the long run influence if they do not determine the prices of oats, barley and other coarse grains, this policy is tending to lower the relative position of agriculture in our whole economy. If that is true, and I believe it is, that step is introducing the first major deflationary factor in our Canadian economy. That is

why the price the farmer should get for his wheat today should be a fair price, and' not less than a fair price.
Fifth, with further respect to its domestic wheat policy, the government is not only getting ready to let agriculture fall back into an inferior position in our economy, but is holding back a portion of the farmers' money for five years. That is a major objection I have to this bill; and that is a feature of this bill we are going to try to have amended. We intend to fight that feature of this bill with all our capacity and endeavour to have it adjusted. If $1.55 is a fair price for Canadian wheat, there is no excuse for not giving it to the Canadian farmer, either in the form of an initial price or if the government still requires that he take less-it is $1.35 now or twenty cents less-then at the end of each crop year the farmer should be given whatever balance there is.
As I have said, the bill should be amended in at least that one respect. We cannot press that amendment at this stage, but we will try in committee to find the place where an amendment of that kind can be proposed. Our amendment will be that any surplus in a year's- operations should be distributed at the end of the year instead of being held until this act expires three or four years from now. In other words, there should be a one-year pool instead of a five-year pool. Let the government hold the surplus money for no more than the end of the crop year; let it give whatever there is back to the farmer each year. It may be a lot; it may be a little; it may be none at all. It may be that in the third and fourth years the price of wheat will be down and the surpluses will have to be used up in order to keep the average up to $1.35.
There are two new features in this bill. One is the power to limit the acreage of wheat and to limit deliveries from each acre and the second is the power to hold back the farmer's money for his participation certificates until this legislation expires in 1950. This it does in the hope that there will be some money left; in the hope that it will have enough to avert possible losses. The initial price guaranteed under this bill of $1.35 is a gamble against a possible drop in prices, but it does not guarantee a stable parity price. It either does that or it does not. I think any careful student of agriculture will agree that it does not. The only hope of the government getting a fair return to farmers under this measure is that there will be at least a twenty-eent increase over the $1.35 payment during the whole five years of this contract. Personally I do not believe that that will be so or

Austiia
anything approaching it. In any event it is money which belongs to the farmer, it does not belong to the government.
Either the first payment should be a parity payment, which is now about $1.55 a bushel; or, if the government will not make it that, then it at least should see that the balances left at the end of each crop year are paid to the farmer and not held for five years.
That, in brief, is our attitude toward this measure and the general question of marketing wheat and other coarse grains. That is our attitude with respect to one particular feature of this bill-the payment yearly of the participation certificates. We think the government should not hold the farmer's money for five years, but should pay him every year the difference between what it receives for the sale of his grain and what it ras paid him as an initial price.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to proceed at any length in the few minutes that are left tonight and I shall in a moment move the adjournment of the debate. However, I should like to reply to the last statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) to the effect that the initial price of $1.35 a bushel was a mere gamble. The initial price of $1.35 a bushel was not a gamble in any sense. It was arrived at by taking the average marketings of wheat over a long period in Canada and calculating that if that wheat was marketed at $155 for the first two years of the contract, 'taking into consideration the fact that one year's wheat had already been marketed at a price of at least $1.55 and the further fact that it would be marketed for another two years at $1.55 at least, then should the price drop to the minimum price of $1.25 provided in the contract for the third year, and if it dropped again to $1 in the fourth year, there would be enough money obtained for the wheat to pay the farmer $1.35 a bushel without any person in Canada outside the farmers paying one cent of it.
In other words, the farmer of western Canada who produces this wheat would not be depending upon the taxpayers in eastern Canada, either in its cities or on its farms, for one cent of the payment wdiich included $1.35 a bushel. That is no gamble; that is a basic fact in connection with this contract. It makes it one of interest to the western farmer who produces the wheat. It is one which we ask the members of this house to support, on the understanding that it is a policy in which the western farmer believes.
If I may be permitted to adjourn the debate at this point I shall continue tomorrow.
On motion of Mr. Gardiner the debate was adj ourned.
